articles.title: Solana treasury Forward Industries flashes a 30% SOL discount, with a catch
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Forward’s preliminary Nov. 9 snapshot implies a 29.7% discount using common shares, versus 2.4% with its broadest count.
- Forward’s one-cent sponsor warrants have share-price hurdles, so the broad share count does not establish immediate issuance.
- Forward’s common shareholders cannot redeem stock for SOL, adding ownership and financing considerations to the apparent NAV discount.
Forward Industries' Nov. 10 update puts the Solana treasury company's shares at a 29.7% discount to net assets using common shares alone.
Counting all the potential shares in the same disclosure, that discount shrinks to 2.4%. The difference is who could eventually share in the assets.
The share count is key almost as much as the treasury for investors comparing Nasdaq-listed FWDI with buying Solana directly.
The capitalization update uses a $5.53 share price and $600.2 million of net asset value (NAV). Forward's accompanying 8-K says the figures are preliminary, unaudited, and incomplete.
Three discounts for three share counts
Dividing the same net assets among more potential shares produces three distinct comparisons:
| November 9 basis | Share count | NAV per share | Calculated discount | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Common shares | 76,288,215 | $7.87 | 29.7% | 
| In-the-money fully diluted | 90,300,322 | $6.65 | 16.8% | 
| Fully diluted | 105,933,854 | $5.67 | 2.4% | 
Each discount is calculated as 1 minus the share price divided by NAV per share, using unrounded values.
The middle count already recognizes substantial claims beyond issued common stock: 12.27 million vested warrants with a displayed exercise price of $0.00, 689,010 options and 1.05 million unvested restricted stock units. It includes unvested options as well as vested ones.
Using the displayed prices for the two in-the-money option categories would add about $3.4 million if both groups vested and exercised for cash. With price, share count, and everything else fixed, that lifts the calculated discount to about 17.3%.
The largest addition between the middle and broadest counts is 13.38 million advisor and lead-investor warrants with a one-cent exercise price. Other additions include out-of-the-money options and warrants, plus 875,324 unvested performance stock units.
The accompanying prospectus to Forward's Nov. 9 filing describes three equal tranches requiring closing prices at 150%, 200% and 250% of the placement purchase price for 20 of 30 trading days after the relevant registration effectiveness.
Against the disclosed $18.50 purchase price, those trigger levels work out to $27.75, $37 and $46.25, subject to applicable adjustments.
If all 13.38 million warrants were exercised for cash at one cent, Forward would receive only about $134,000. The advisor warrant form and lead-investor warrant form also permit cashless exercise.
Forward's June-quarter filing describes management restricted stock units vesting over four years with service conditions, while performance units require both service and company performance measures.
The broadest count captures these potential ownership claims, but does not establish when, or whether, all will become issued shares.
A treasury metric is not a Solana withdrawal right
Forward's reported NAV combines $755.9 million of SOL and equivalents, $26.6 million of other digital assets and $5.25 million of cash and marketable securities, less $187.5 million of institutional debt.
The 8.73 million Solana-equivalent balance includes fwdSOL and pledged SOL and excludes borrowed SOL.
That debt is already deducted in the NAV calculation, and Forward warns that declines in pledged SOL could require additional collateral or repayment.
The company's common-share terms provide no redemption provisions, so its reported 0.0824 SOL per fully diluted share is a treasury exposure metric. A discount alone supplies no contractual route to collect the difference.
November's amendment added Barclays to the existing up-to-$4 billion equity sales program. The prospectus reports only 529,257 shares sold for about $12.1 million gross through Nov. 6.
Token ownership is the exposure for direct SOL buyers, while the judgment also concerns management's use of assets and financing, and which contingent claims to include for FWDI buyers.
The middle measure leaves a meaningful dated discount, while the broadest leaves little cushion.

articles.title: Anthropic’s new AI leads freelance benchmarks, yet fails 58% of the tasks
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Fable 5.2 leads Scale’s Remote Labor Index at 41.30%, ahead of Opus 5.5’s 21.25% project pass rate.
- RLI measures complete deliverables against professional reference work, giving practical AI capability a test grounded in freelance projects.
- Current spending and human support remain unresolved.
Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 ranks first on the Remote Labor Index, a test of complete freelance projects, with 41.3% of its deliverables judged to meet a professional reference standard.
Scale’s Nov. 12 leaderboard lists Fable 5.2 at 41.3%, ahead of the next-highest model, Opus 5.5 at 21.25%. Anthropic reported the result in its Nov. 9 release announcement, labeling the RLI score “High effort” and indicating that safeguards were enabled.
The original RLI paper, submitted in October 2025 by researchers from the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI, describes a dataset of 240 projects across 23 freelance work categories. Each includes a brief, the files needed to complete the task, and a professional human-reference deliverable.
The selected projects include documents, audio, video, 3D models, and computer-aided design files. That range makes file production and finished-product quality part of the challenge, alongside understanding what the client requested.
The researchers’ original evaluation method uses trained human reviewers to inspect the AI’s work against the brief and reference deliverable.
Independent evaluations and majority voting determine outcomes, and a project passes when the AI’s deliverable satisfies the brief at least as well as the reference, at a quality a reasonable client would accept.
A useful prototype or a partial result can therefore fall below the pass threshold, even when it demonstrates relevant skills. Passing demands a deliverable that clears the professional reference standard.
What the Anthropic score leaves open
Fable 5.2’s score still leaves most evaluated projects below that acceptance threshold.
The original study excludes work that inherently requires client interaction, teamwork, or physical labor, as well as projects whose outcome must be awaited before it can be evaluated. Those exclusions limit how broadly the result can apply to the wider remote-work economy.
Anthropic’s release page specifies High effort, but does not establish the precise RLI execution setup, spending per project, or amount of human support.
RLI provides a demanding definition of success for a business assessing AI’s usefulness: carrying an assignment through to an inspectable product, with professional work setting the acceptance standard.

articles.title: South Korea to Allow Crypto Withdrawal Freezes Over Suspected Hacks
articles.text:
South Korea to permit crypto withdrawal freezes during hacking threats
The move follows recent security incidents involving South Korean crypto exchanges, including GOPAX’s precautionary suspension of services and a $70,000 hot-wallet breach at Prabang.
South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) plans to allow crypto exchanges to suspend deposits and withdrawals when hacking is suspected, rather than waiting until a breach is confirmed, amid a push for stronger industry security.
On Thursday, the FSC said it would issue a no-action letter permitting preventive suspensions under certain conditions. Current rules prohibit exchanges from blocking withdrawals without legitimate grounds and explicitly allow restrictions only when a hacking incident is clearly established.
The regulator also called for round-the-clock monitoring and incident response, higher cold-wallet holdings, and stronger insurance coverage and reserves. The FSC said exchanges unable to monitor continuously would process deposits and withdrawals only during staffed hours and notify users in advance.
The move follows recent security incidents involving South Korean exchanges. On Friday, crypto exchange GOPAX suspended trading, deposits and standard withdrawals after receiving a hacking threat, although a representative said no breach had occurred. On Oct. 24, trading platform Prabang suspended services after detecting abnormal hot-wallet withdrawals, reporting about $70,000 in losses.
In October, the FSC identified cybersecurity deficiencies at 130 of 555 financial companies reviewed nationwide. It separately identified GOPAX operator Streami and Prabang among 16 companies involved in earlier security incidents.
Related: South Korea lawmakers mull pushing crypto tax implementation to 2029

articles.title: Helius encrypts Solana transfers without removing operator trust
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Helius launched confidential Solana transfers on Nov. 10, hiding assets and amounts while leaving wallet addresses visible.
- The documented default prover handles secret inputs inside an attested AWS Nitro enclave, while the wallet retains signing authority.
- Wallets can check enclave measurements and encryption keys, while code review and deployment policy remain separate trust dependencies.
Helius launched its permissionless Privacy Ring on Solana mainnet on Nov. 10 with encrypted payment assets and amounts, while sender and recipient wallet addresses remain visible.
Its documented default prover, the service that constructs zero-knowledge proofs, adds a hardware requirement where secret transaction inputs are processed inside an attested AWS Nitro enclave, an isolated computing environment.
Solana can check that a transfer satisfies the protocol’s rules, but protecting the inputs while that proof is made depends on the prover’s isolation, code, and deployment policies.
The practical question for wallet developers integrating the launch is which of those protections their software can verify.
What reaches the Solana prover
Helius’s wallet integration guide says proof generation needs plaintext inputs covering the complete transaction data and nullifier keys. It identifies an attested AWS Nitro enclave as the SDKs’ default prover.
The protocol specification lists private inputs including the asset, amount, blinding values, and nullifier secret for notes being spent, along with paths proving those notes belong to the state tree. The proof also includes output assets, amounts, and blinding values.
Those inputs become readable to the proving code inside the enclave, and the documented client protects them from the host operator by encrypting requests to a key held by the attested enclave.
The nullifier secret also derives the markers used to prevent repeat spending. In the native wallet integration, the wallet retains the signing key, and the TypeScript SDK leaves signing of the finished Solana transaction with the application’s signer.
Helius documents local decryption, which keeps the viewing key on the device, and delegated decryption, which shares a viewing key with an authorized provider. Delegation gives that provider read access to balances and history, without granting spending authority.
AWS describes Nitro Enclaves as isolated environments whose memory the parent instance’s processes or administrators cannot access. Enclaves have no persistent storage, interactive access, or external networking.
AWS’s signed document contains cryptographic fingerprints of its image and software. The documented Privacy Rings checks verify the certificate chain, challenge response and freshness, approved measurements, and the binding of the request-encryption key.
The tagged SDK refuses a remote prover request without one, before making an HTTP call. A wallet can pin a reviewed release policy or use a network policy authenticated by the SDK’s pinned signers. Signed policies refresh during attestation and expire after use.
Where Solana's deployment trust remains
A wallet can automatically check that the enclave matches an approved software image and encryption key, yet deciding which image to approve still requires confidence in the code and its reviewers.
The Nitro deployment guide says the measured image includes the prover, startup script, certificate bundle, allowed external hosts, indexer URL, and KMS key identity. Its design uses AWS Key Management Service to release the shared encryption seed only to matching attested enclaves.
The guide says clients cannot read the KMS key policy and rely on the operator’s deployment for that guarantee. It identifies AWS KMS, AWS Support, Nitro hardware, and the operator as trust roots during initial policy binding.
Even correctly encrypted requests leave metadata visible to the parent, such as paths, queries, timing, and sizes. The path reveals the proof’s circuit shape.
The versioned TEE guide records a mainnet build based on v0.6.0-alpha, with measured-build provenance, distinct from the ts-sdk-v0.8.0-alpha documentation tag.
The specification allows client-side proofs, and the repository supplies localnet tooling and downloadable prover binaries.
Helius’s launch announcement says Certora, zkSecurity, and OtterSec audited programs and circuits. Its security page lists Certora in October and zkSecurity in August, while marking OtterSec as awaiting a report.
The launch gives wallet developers a trust decision on which code and deployment policy they approve to handle proof inputs.

articles.title: Binance Security Chief Warned of Hack Tactic Before $6.3B Theft
articles.text:
Binance CSO unwittingly foreshadowed $6.3B hack tactic months before attack
In a July interview, Binance chief security officer Jimmy Su explained how fake coding assessments could compromise employee devices, a tactic later used in the exchange’s record-breaking hack.
Months before Binance lost $6.3 billion to a hack, its chief security officer described to Cointelegraph how a fake job interview could give attackers a foothold inside the exchange — closely resembling one of the entry methods later used against the exchange.
During a July interview about Binance’s response to rising security threats, Jimmy Su told Cointelegraph that fake job interviews were “something we worry about a lot internally,” explaining how attackers could tailor a job opportunity to an employee before persuading them to run code as part of a technical assessment.
“And once that gets executed, the device is compromised and then they can start harvesting credentials,” Su said, adding that attackers could then use that to penetrate further into the network.
Su’s detailed warning about malicious coding assessments was not included in Cointelegraph’s July coverage, but takes on new significance following the biggest crypto exchange hack in history.
In September, a Binance software engineer downloaded a malicious coding assignment onto his work computer during a fake job interview. That compromise became part of the multistage attack that culminated in October’s theft, according to Binance’s preliminary investigation.
During the interview with Cointelegraph, Su had also anticipated why security tools might miss such a trap. A technical assessment could involve seemingly legitimate steps, such as downloading a code repository from GitHub, he explained in July.
“Each step is actually legitimate on its own. So a lot of the anti-virus tools may not be able to detect it and flag it,” he said.
Binance’s investigation subsequently described a similar detection failure, saying the assignment’s setup process executed malware that evaded its endpoint security tools through obfuscation and other evasion techniques.
Binance said onus is on the company to detect attacks
Su told Cointelegraph that it was Binance’s responsibility to contain the risk when employees pursued outside opportunities on work computers.
“Of course employees can explore outside opportunities. What we do worry about is that they do so on the company device,” he said. If an employee fell for a fake interview, he added, “the onus is on us to detect it,” and to “stop the actual execution of that code.”
Related: North Korean hackers create memecoins to launder funds from Binance hack: Elliptic
Binance was already testing employees against fake recruiters. Su said its internal red team had been conducting monthly phishing simulations for three to four years, with remedial training for employees who failed.
“In the beginning, the security hygiene left a lot to be desired. But after this amount of time, the company has improved significantly,” he said.
Kevin Gibson of recruitment firm Proof of Search told Cointelegraph that the threat is also changing how some crypto employers assess prospective hires, with clients increasingly wanting to know whether candidates have been met in person.
“A number of our clients are now asking us straight up whether we’ve met a candidate in person,” Gibson said, adding that candidates personally met by a third-party recruiter have an advantage.
Employees, like in Binance’s case, can also become targets.
“In crypto, a dodgy job offer or a ‘quick catch-up call’ can be the first step in a multimillion-dollar hit,” he said.
Binance blocks a North Korean cyber threat every five days
Binance said it blocked 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threats so far this year, which is roughly one attack every five days.
Following October’s attack, Binance said it had tightened device controls, rebuilt affected wallet systems and internal AI tooling, strengthened access controls and revoked compromised credentials.
It also said it was increasing investment in endpoint protection and developer-environment security, and engaging independent cybersecurity experts to review the incident. Some technical details and security measures would remain confidential, it said.
