articles.title: Nguồn gốc dị không tưởng của các từ ngữ được dùng phổ biến hiện nay, bạn chắc chắn sẽ bất ngờ
articles.text:
Ngày nay, những từ tiếng Anh như "deadline" được sử dụng phổ biến trong giới văn phòng. Vậy nguồn gốc của chúng từ đâu mà ra và có gì thú vị?
Deadline là từ tiếng Anh có nguồn gốc từ Hoa Kỳ, cụ thể hơn là từ những người có tham gia Nội chiến. Nó được đề cập đến lần đầu tiên trong phiên tòa xét xử Henry Wirz, một chỉ huy khét tiếng ở nhà tù khốc liệt nhất mà phe Liên minh đã lập ra.
Trong phiên tòa này, Warz đã nói với các cai ngục về một đường dân tưởng tượng xung quanh nhà tù và không vượt qua vạch này, họ sẽ được an toàn. Ngược lại, nếu vượt qua vạch này, tù nhân sẽ bị bắn ngay lập tức. Vạch giới hạn mà Warz đặt ra được gọi là "deadline".
Ở thời hiện đại, deadline không còn mang ý tiêu cực như ban đầu mà được dùng để nói về thời hạn hoàn thành một công việc nào đó.
Avocado trong tiếng Anh hiện đại có nghĩa là quả bơ, một giống trái cây có vỏ màu tím thẫm. Tuy nhiên, nguồn gốc của tên gọi này lại bắt nguồn từ Aztec. Bơ là loại trái cây ăn kèm bánh mì nướng được nhiều người yêu thích, do đó mà người Aztec xem nó như thực phẩm quý, họ gọi nó là "ahuakatl". Điều khiến nhiều người bất ngờ ở đây là việc từ "ahuakatll" còn có thêm nghĩa phụ khá nhạy cảm, nó được dùng để chỉ bộ phận sinh dục của nam giới.
Ngày nay, ai cũng quen với việc sử dụng từ robot để gọi tên những cỗ máy hoạt động tự động bằng kim loại và có trí thông minh nhân tạo. Trong văn hóa đại chúng, hẳn các nhân vật WALL-E hay Kẻ hủy diệt không còn quá xa lạ. Tuy nhiên, nguồn gốc của tên gọi robot này lại không mấy vui vẻ. Trong tiếng Czech cổ, "rabu" có nghĩa là "nô lệ". Theo thời gian, từ này dần bị biến nghĩa thành "robotnik" có nghĩa là "công nhân bị ép lao động". Nhiều người vẫn nghĩ robot là nô lệ của con người, và quả thật người ta đã chọn cho chúng một cái tên thể hiện rõ suy nghĩ như thế.
Geek là từ lóng dùng để chỉ những người quá thông minh đến mức có vẻ hơi ngờ nghệch trong những giao tiếp thường ngày. Geek vốn là một từ trong tiếng Hà Lan. Cho đến nay người ta vẫn tranh cãi về việc geek có phải là một từ mang ý xúc phạm hay không (vẫn có những người tự nhận là geek và tỏ ra tự hào với việc này). Tuy nhiên, dù ý kiến có ra sao, họ đều phải đồng ý rằng từ gốc của geek mang hàm ý không hề thân thiện.
Vào những năm 1500, "gek" có nghĩa là "kẻ ngu ngốc, đơn giản" trong tiếng Hà Lan. Sau đó, vào những năm 1900, geek lại mang một nghĩa mới khi các rạp xiếc trở nên nở rộ ở Hoa kỳ, nó có nghĩa là "sự quá đản". Cuối cùng, vào những năm 80, nó lại có thêm nghĩa bóng nhằm để chỉ các "thanh thiếu niên không được yêu quý."
Quarantine có nghĩa là cách ly. Nó bắt nguồn từ tiếng Ý. Vào thế kỷ 14, khi các tàu buôn về Venice sau những hải trình xa xôi, các quan chức ở thành phố không muốn họ lây bệnh lạ cho dân chúng nên đã đề ra quy định cách ly. Theo đó, khi tàu trở về từ các khu vực có dịch hạch, các thủy thủ trên tàu buộc phải ở ngoài cảng Venice trong 40 ngày, để đảm bảo không có thủy thủ nào bị nhiễm bệnh. Từ quy định này mà trong tiếng Ý có thêm cụm từ "aranta giorno", có nghĩa là "khoảng thời gian 40 ngày".

articles.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
articles.text:
Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- University of York
- Summary:
- A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.
- Share:
Deep inside South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, scientists have uncovered a surprising clue about an extinct human relative that lived hundreds of thousands of years ago. For the first time, researchers have recovered and studied ancient proteins from Homo naledi fossils, revealing evidence that the cave may have contained an exclusively female burial site.
The discovery, published in the journal Cell, raises an extraordinary possibility. The cave could represent the earliest known burial location reserved for one sex by a human relative other than Homo sapiens.
Homo naledi lived approximately 335,000 to 241,000 years ago and has fascinated scientists since its discovery in 2013. This extinct species combined primitive features resembling those of apes with other characteristics more closely associated with modern humans.
A Strange Mystery Hidden in Ancient Human Fossils
One of the biggest puzzles surrounding Homo naledi involves the remarkably similar appearance of adult fossils recovered from the cave's Dinaledi Chamber. For more than a decade, researchers have struggled to explain why these individuals showed so little of the physical variation normally associated with differences between males and females.
To investigate, an international research team involving the University of York, the University of Copenhagen, and more than 10 other institutions turned to proteins preserved in the ancient remains.
The scientists used a technique involving gentle acid etching to recover tiny protein fragments known as peptides from fossilized tooth enamel. This approach allowed them to collect samples while minimizing damage to the valuable fossils. In total, they examined 23 teeth belonging to at least 20 different individuals.
The researchers specifically searched for Amelogenin-Y, a protein produced from a gene on the male Y chromosome. Surprisingly, they found no evidence of this male-specific marker.
To verify that their findings were reliable, specialists at the University of York's chemistry facility examined the amino acids in the samples. Their analysis confirmed that the proteins were genuinely ancient rather than the result of contamination from modern sources.
Could Homo naledi Have Had an All-Female Burial Site?
Dr. Marc Dickinson, from the University of York's Department of Chemistry, said: "The lack of male markers with the group is truly fascinating. It is incredibly exciting to gain a window not only into the biology of our ancestors, but also into how they lived.
"These findings offer rare insights into a culture that has, until now, been difficult to access directly. Advances in ancient protein analysis are opening the door to a far richer and more nuanced understanding of ancient hominins."
The results raise important questions about how Homo naledi individuals lived, organized their communities, and treated their dead. If the Dinaledi Chamber was intentionally used only for females, it could point to surprisingly elaborate social customs among these ancient human relatives.
Such a practice might even suggest symbolic burial traditions once believed to be exclusive to Homo sapiens, or modern humans.
However, the researchers emphasize that an all-female burial site is not the only possible interpretation of the evidence.
Another explanation involves the genetics of Homo naledi itself. If the population lived in extreme isolation, the gene responsible for producing Amelogenin-Y could have undergone a mutation or disappeared entirely.
Under that scenario, some of the individuals could actually have been male, even though their teeth did not contain the protein normally used to identify them.
Ancient Tooth Enamel Opens a New Window Into Human Evolution
The ability to recover proteins from fossils this old is particularly valuable because tooth enamel can protect biological material for extraordinarily long periods.
Palesa Madupe, who carried out the research during her postdoctoral work at the University of Copenhagen, explained why teeth offer such an important source of evidence.
"Unlike those found in other remains like bone fragments, proteins in tooth enamel are preserved because dental enamel -- the hardest tissue in the human body -- shields proteins from environmental contamination even for millions of years.
"This makes them ideal carriers of genetic information from deep time. Our study helps in the long-standing mystery of why Homo naledi lacked significant variation; it's probably because they could have all belonged to one sex."
The research represents the largest collection of individuals from an extinct hominin species ever examined using ancient protein analysis.
Whether the fossils belong entirely to females or include males with an unusual genetic signature, the discovery provides an important new perspective on Homo naledi. It also demonstrates how proteins preserved in ancient teeth can reveal clues about extinct human relatives that their bones alone cannot provide.
As researchers continue investigating the mystery, the findings could reshape our understanding of the social lives and possible burial traditions of ancient human species.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of York. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Palesa P. Madupe, Alberto J. Taurozzi, Claire Koenig, Ioannis Patramanis, Fazeelah Munir, Marc R. Dickinson, Meaghan Mackie, Gaudry Troché, Glendon Parker, Pelagia Kyriakidou, Patrick Mahoney, Gina McFarlane, Bernhard Zipfel, Jürgen Cox, Kirsty Penkman, Lauren Schroeder, Rebecca R. Ackermann, Jesper V. Olsen, John Hawks, Lee Berger, Enrico Cappellini. Proteomic analysis of dental enamel from 20 Homo naledi individuals shows no male markers. Cell, 2026; 189 (14): 4415 DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.05.044

articles.title: A radical theory says the universe is twice as old as we thought
articles.text:
A radical theory says the universe is twice as old as we thought
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- University of Ottawa
- Summary:
- A provocative new cosmological model suggests the Universe could be 26.7 billion years old and might not need dark matter or dark energy to explain its behavior. University of Ottawa researchers tested the theory against several major astronomical observations, finding that it could explain galaxy rotation, cosmic expansion, and the formation of early elements.
- Share:
A radical alternative to the standard picture of the cosmos is gaining attention after researchers at the University of Ottawa reported that it successfully matched several important astronomical observations. The model suggests that the Universe could be 26.7 billion years old, nearly twice the widely accepted age of 13.8 billion years, and that neither dark matter nor dark energy is needed to explain its behavior.
If further research supports these findings, the theory could offer a very different explanation for how the Universe evolved. It may also help resolve one of modern astronomy's most puzzling discoveries: the existence of surprisingly large and mature galaxies at a time when the conventional model suggests they should barely have begun forming.
A Universe Without Dark Matter or Dark Energy
Throughout 2025 and 2026, Rajendra Gupta, an adjunct professor in the University of Ottawa's Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras evaluated an alternative cosmological framework known as CCC+TL against several major astronomical observations.
The name stands for “covarying coupling constants plus tired light.” Rather than relying on dark matter and dark energy, the model proposes that some of the effects attributed to these mysterious components could result from changes over time in fundamental physical constants. These constants help determine how particles and forces interact.
For decades, astronomers have searched for direct evidence of dark matter and dark energy. Dark matter is thought to provide additional gravity that helps explain how galaxies move and how large cosmic structures hold together. Dark energy is the name given to whatever is causing the expansion of the Universe to accelerate. Although extensive observations support their gravitational and cosmological effects, neither component has been directly identified.
The prevailing cosmological framework, called ΛCDM, incorporates both. Despite its success in explaining a wide range of observations, it faces questions raised by the discovery of unexpectedly developed galaxies in the early Universe.
“Most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations,” Professor Gupta says. “A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published Cosmic Microwave Background challenge.”
Testing such a fundamentally different theory requires more than adjusting the standard model. CCC+TL modifies the Einstein and Friedmann equations, which describe gravity and how the Universe expands. As a result, Gupta and Samaras had to develop equations and computer programs specifically adapted to their model for each test.
New Cosmology Model Passes Several Key Tests
The researchers report that CCC+TL produced results consistent with several major astronomical measurements. One important test involved the light elements created shortly after the Big Bang, including hydrogen and helium. The alternative model predicted abundances that matched those calculated using the standard cosmological framework.
It also agreed with cosmic chronometer measurements, which allow astronomers to reconstruct the history of cosmic expansion by comparing the ages of galaxies at different distances. These measurements provide an independent way to examine how the expansion rate has changed over billions of years.
Another significant test focused on the motion of galaxies. In a recent study published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the researchers examined all 175 galaxies in the SPARC database. They found that their model could reproduce the observed rotation curves without invoking dark matter.
Rotation curves describe how quickly stars and gas orbit at different distances from the centers of galaxies. Under conventional gravity, the visible matter alone generally cannot explain these motions, which is one of the major reasons scientists believe dark matter exists.
The team also investigated time dilation in observations of supernovae. Time dilation refers to the apparent stretching of events over time when viewed across vast cosmic distances. Their analysis offered additional support for CCC+TL, although the research paper remains under review.
Explaining Galaxy Motions Without Invisible Matter
The researchers also examined the Bullet Cluster, a famous system of colliding galaxy clusters that provides some of the strongest observational evidence for dark matter.
In this system, most of the ordinary matter is concentrated in extremely hot gas that emits X-rays. However, observations show that much of the gravitational effect is associated with the galaxies rather than the gas. The standard explanation is that invisible dark matter passed through the collision along with the galaxies.
Under CCC+TL, the additional gravitational effect predicted by the model also follows the galaxies instead of the hot gas, but without requiring dark matter. The researchers emphasize that this result is only an initial proof of concept and that more detailed investigations are necessary.
“Observations attributed to dark matter and dark energy likely originate from covarying coupling constants,” adds Professor Gupta, who examines this possibility further in a separate paper exploring the origin of dark matter and dark energy.
Could the Universe Be Twice as Old as We Thought?
Perhaps the most intriguing implication of the model involves the earliest galaxies ever observed.
Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered galaxies that appear surprisingly massive and mature for their early place in cosmic history. Their existence has prompted questions about how quickly stars and galaxies could have formed after the Big Bang.
CCC+TL offers a possible answer by giving the early Universe substantially more time to develop.
In the standard cosmological model, the Universe was approximately 300 million years old during the period known as cosmic dawn, when the first generations of stars and galaxies were emerging. At the same observed redshift, however, CCC+TL would place the Universe's age at roughly 4.6 billion years.
Redshift measures how much light from a distant object has shifted toward longer, redder wavelengths. Astronomers use it to study distant galaxies and investigate earlier stages of cosmic history.
Under the alternative model, galaxies observed at extremely high redshifts would have had billions of additional years to grow. The researchers calculate that early galaxies would be approximately 12 times larger in both size and mass than predicted by standard cosmology, according to findings published in Galaxies 13, 115.
“Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies,” Professor Gupta explains. “We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached.”
James Webb Could Put the Radical Theory to the Test
Upcoming observations could provide an important opportunity to investigate this prediction.
The James Webb Space Telescope's GLIMPSE program aims to search for extremely distant galaxies, potentially reaching redshifts greater than 50. These observations would probe an exceptionally early period in the Universe's history under the standard cosmological framework.
According to conventional models, there may not have been enough time for large galaxies to assemble at such extreme redshifts. The CCC+TL model does not impose the same restriction because its cosmic timeline allows substantially more time for galaxies to develop.
Finding galaxies at these distances could therefore provide another important way to compare the competing explanations. However, such discoveries would not, by themselves, establish that the alternative model is correct.
Although the researchers report encouraging results across several major cosmological tests, CCC+TL remains an unconventional proposal that requires further independent examination. The standard cosmological model continues to explain a broad range of astronomical observations, and any replacement must ultimately demonstrate comparable or greater success.
For Gupta, the latest findings provide a reason to continue investigating the possibility that the Universe operates differently than scientists currently assume.
“The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the Universe beyond ΛCDM limits,” concludes Professor Gupta.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Ottawa. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Rajendra P. Gupta, Nikolaos Samaras. A Big Bang Nucleosynthesis Consistency Test of the CCC TL Cosmology. Universe, 2026; 12 (7): 193 DOI: 10.3390/universe12070193

articles.title: Nổi da gà với loài động vật chân bụng có áo giáp sắt
articles.text:
Sự đa dạng sinh học hiện nay đã đủ khiến con người phải kinh ngạc, nhưng chúng ta phải biết rằng nhiều sinh vật đã tiến hóa từ rất lâu, để tồn tại trên trái đất và thích nghi với môi trường trái đất, mỗi sinh vật cũng phát triển những khả năng khác nhau.
Để có thể ăn nhiều thức ăn hơn, chúng đã phát triển những móng vuốt rất sắc bén, và tốc độ chạy của chúng ngày càng tăng, và nhiều con mồi đã học được một số bản năng để tự tồn tại, chẳng hạn như một số động vật sẽ đổi màu, một số động vật sẽ ngụy trang, và trong số nhiều loài động vật, động vật hiệu quả nhất để bảo vệ mình là động vật giáp xác, trong tự nhiên, chẳng hạn như cua, rùa và các động vật khác, chúng đã tiến hóa, có vỏ rất cứng.
Theo thống kê, hiện nay trên trái đất có hơn 20.000 loại động vật giáp xác, loài giáp xác này thường không có thiên địch, vì khi kẻ thù đến ăn chúng sẽ thụt vào vỏ và không có cách nào để ăn chúng. Có một sinh vật trong số đó, chúng có vỏ cứng nhất trên thế giới, vỏ của sinh vật này được làm bằng sắt.
Rất sâu dưới đáy Ấn Độ Dương, gần miệng phun thủy nhiệt nóng nực, nơi những dòng nước nóng phun trào thành những cột khói đen và cao, có loài động vật chân bụng kỳ lạ sinh sống với tên khoa học là Chrysomallon squamiferum. Đây là một loài ốc sên thủy nhiệt thuộc họ động vật thân mềm sống dưới đáy biển sâu.
Người ta cho rằng ngay cả viên đạn cũng không thể xuyên qua vỏ của loài ốc này, phạm vi hoạt động của loài ốc này là hơn 2.000 mét dưới biển, nói chung loại ốc này sống ở miệng phun thủy nhiệt. Đây là nơi có áp suất nước, nhiệt độ và độ axit cao, trong khi hàm lượng oxy rất thấp. Chính vì vỏ của chúng rất cứng nên chúng có thể chịu được áp lực rất lớn.
Môi trường sống ngặt nghèo đã khiến loài ốc sên chân vảy tiến hóa theo hướng phát triết một bộ áo giáp độc đáo. Cụ thể, vỏ của ốc sên chân vảy gồm ba lớp, mỗi lớp được cho là có một chức năng bảo vệ riêng.
Ốc sên thủy nhiệt sống dưới đáy biển sâu. 
Lớp ngoài cùng dày khoảng 30 micromet, được làm bằng sulfua sắt. Lớp này có thể vỡ khi bị va đập nhưng đó cũng là cách để ốc hấp thụ năng lượng, đồng thời làm nản lòng bất cứ kẻ thù nào muốn tấn công nó.
Lớp giữa là sừng hữu cơ, tương tự như lớp phủ bằng protein mỏng ở trên các loại vỏ ốc khác. Đây cũng là lớp dày nhất trong ba lớp và cũng là dày nhất (khoảng 150 micromet), có tác dụng như một tấm đệm hữu cơ "giảm đau" cho ốc.
Lớp trong cùng là aragonite - một dạng canxi carbonat thường được tìm thấy trong vỏ của nhiều loài động vật thân mềm và san hô khác nhau.
Hai bên chân của ốc sên chân vẩy cực kỳ khác thường, khi được bọc bằng hàng trăm mảnh vụn khoáng hóa sắt, bao gồm sắt sunfua greigite và pyrit. Những chiếc vảy này không có ở bất kỳ loài ốc nào khác trên Trái đất. Mục đích của chúng có thể là để bảo vệ hoặc là kết quả của sự lắng đọng chất thải sulfua độc hại từ các sinh vật nội cộng sinh
Ốc sên thủy nhiệt.
Môi trường sống khắc nghiệt khiến ốc phải thích nghi với chiếc vỏ gồm 3 lớp.
Về sinh dưỡng, ốc sên chân vảy là loài sống cộng sinh bắt buộc với vi khuẩn trong suốt cuộc đời. Chúng thu thập tất cả chất dinh dưỡng từ quá trình tự dưỡng hóa học của vi khuẩn nội cộng sinh.
Về sinh sản, đây là loài lưỡng tính đồng thời (có cả cơ quan sinh dục đực và cái, cùng chín một thời điểm). Dù chưa có chứng cứ, người ta phỏng đoán ấu trùng của chúng có giai đoạn trôi nổi như sinh vật phù du trước khi bám vào đáy biển.
Như vậy, mỗi lớp trong chiếc vỏ dày của ốc đều có vai trò quan trọng đóng góp vào sự hiệu quả về mặt phòng ngự của ốc. Các nhà khoa học cho biết đây là loài sinh vật duy nhất trên Trái đất được biết đến với khả năng sử dụng sắt trong chính bộ vỏ của mình để làm lớp bảo vệ. Quân đội Mỹ hiện đang nghiên cứu để chế tạo loại áo giáp mới hiệu quả.
Trong Sách Độ của IUCN, ốc sên chân vảy được xếp vào danh sách các loài Nguy cấp. Nguy cơ cho sự tồn vong của chúng chủ yếu đến từ những tác động của hoạt động khai thác mỏ dưới biển sâu.

articles.title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
articles.text:
Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
- Date:
- November 10, 2026
- Source:
- University of Pennsylvania
- Summary:
- A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.
- Share:
A specially engineered chewing gum could offer an unexpected new weapon against viruses and bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. In laboratory tests using samples from cancer patients, researchers found that extracts from the gum reduced levels of human papillomavirus, or HPV, by as much as 93%. An enhanced version also nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species while leaving beneficial bacteria unharmed.
The findings, reported in Scientific Reports, suggest that this experimental approach could eventually help prevent certain infections and support existing cancer treatments. Researchers believe the plant-based technology could also provide a more affordable option for patients.
The research was led by Henry Daniell of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Dental Medicine. His team has been exploring ways to use specially engineered plants to produce proteins with potential medical benefits.
Why Scientists Are Targeting Cancer-Linked Microbes
Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that develops in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. It begins in squamous cells, the thin, flat cells that cover many surfaces throughout the body. These cancers can be particularly difficult to treat once they have spread, and patients diagnosed at advanced stages often face poor outcomes.
According to Daniell, recently approved cancer medications have generally failed to produce major improvements in patients' quality of life or their chances of surviving five years after diagnosis. This highlights the continuing need for more effective treatments and new strategies that could help prevent the disease or reduce complications.
One promising area of research involves the microorganisms living in the mouth. Although many oral microbes are harmless or beneficial, certain viruses and bacteria have been associated with the development or progression of head and neck cancers.
The researchers focused on three of these microbes. The first was HPV, a common virus that can cause certain cancers when infections persist. The other two were Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), bacterial species associated with oral disease and poorer outcomes in some cancer patients.
"The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies."
Oropharyngeal cancer affects the middle portion of the throat, including areas such as the tonsils and base of the tongue. Metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has spread beyond its original location, while adjuvant treatments are additional therapies given to improve the effectiveness of primary treatment.
A Chewing Gum Made From Beans Delivers Surprising Results
The new study builds on the team's earlier development of a chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). This gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring protein with antiviral properties.
To investigate its potential benefits, the scientists tested extracts from the gum against microbes found in oral samples collected from patients with head and neck cancer.
The results were striking. The bean gum extracts lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples and by 80% in oral rinse samples. These findings suggest that proteins delivered through a chewing gum could potentially help reduce the presence of a virus associated with certain head and neck cancers.
The team then took the technology a step further by engineering the gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Some antimicrobial peptides can attack and destroy harmful microorganisms, making them promising candidates for new infection treatments.
With this additional ingredient, the researchers found that a single dose of the engineered gum extract reduced the two targeted bacterial species, Pg and Fn, to almost undetectable levels.
Harmful Bacteria Nearly Disappear While Good Bacteria Survive
One of the most encouraging findings was the gum's ability to target harmful bacteria without disrupting the beneficial microorganisms that naturally inhabit the mouth.
The oral microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microscopic organisms living inside the mouth, plays an important role in maintaining oral health. Many of these microbes coexist harmlessly with the body and help maintain a balanced environment.
Some cancer treatments can disturb that balance. Radiation therapy, for example, can reduce populations of beneficial oral bacteria while encouraging the growth of potentially harmful yeast, including Candida albicans.
In contrast, the experimental gum extract sharply reduced the targeted bacteria without affecting the beneficial bacterial populations examined by the researchers. This selectivity could be especially valuable for patients whose oral health has already been affected by cancer or its treatment.
Importantly, the results came from laboratory testing of patient samples rather than clinical trials in which people chewed the gum. Further research will be needed to determine whether the same effects occur in the human mouth and whether reducing these microbes can meaningfully improve cancer outcomes.
Could Chewing Gum Become Part of Cancer Prevention and Treatment?
The researchers believe their findings justify moving the technology toward human clinical trials, particularly because head and neck cancers remain a serious global health challenge.
"Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," says Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission."
Prophylaxis refers to measures taken to prevent disease or infection before it occurs. In this case, the researchers envision a future in which specially designed chewing gum might help limit exposure to harmful microbes or reduce their levels in people already receiving cancer treatment.
Such an approach could offer a relatively simple and potentially inexpensive way to deliver protective proteins directly into the mouth, where the targeted microorganisms are found.
For now, the technology remains experimental, and there is no evidence yet that chewing the gum prevents or treats cancer in humans. Nevertheless, the ability to substantially reduce HPV and nearly eliminate two cancer-associated bacterial species in laboratory tests offers a promising starting point for further investigation.
If future clinical trials confirm its safety and effectiveness, a familiar everyday product could become an unexpected addition to the medical toolkit against dangerous oral infections and cancers.
Henry Daniell is the W.D. Miller Professor in the Department of Basic & Translational Sciences at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.
Other authors are Geetanjali Wakade, Rahul Singh, and Smruti Nair of Penn Dental Medicine; Andrés M. Bur and Sufi M. Thomas of the University of Kansas Medical Center; Eri S. Srivatsan and Marilene B. Wang of the University of California at Los Angeles; and Saroj K. Basak of the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System.
This work was supported by NIH (grant 5-R01-HL 107904-13 awarded to Henry Daniell), the Academic Senate Grant of David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA (the Surgical Education Research program), and National Cancer Institute Cancer Center (Support Grant P30 CA168524).

Ex vivo HNSCC clinical studies using saliva and antiviral or antibacterial chewing gums reveal reduction in carcinogenic microbes. Scientific Reports, 2026; 16 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-39062-w

articles.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke
articles.text:
Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke
- Date:
- November 10, 2026
- Source:
- American Heart Association
- Summary:
- New research involving more than 440,000 Americans links cannabis use to increased cardiovascular risk, with occasional users showing 40% higher odds of reporting a history of stroke. The findings suggest that even infrequent marijuana use may warrant concern, although researchers have not established that cannabis directly causes strokes or heart disease.
- Share:
New preliminary research involving more than 440,000 American adults has uncovered a concerning association between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease, particularly stroke. The findings suggest that even occasional marijuana use may be linked to higher odds of cardiovascular problems, raising new questions about the health effects of a substance that is becoming increasingly common across the United States.
The research, presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, found that the association was not limited to people who frequently used cannabis. It also appeared across different methods of consumption (smoked or edible, etc.). Researchers emphasized that cannabis use should be considered when discussing heart health and stroke prevention.
Scientific Sessions 2026 took place November 6 through 9 in Chicago, bringing together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, clinical advances, and emerging evidence.
Cannabis refers to the plant itself, while marijuana is a commonly used term for cannabis products containing enough THC to produce psychoactive effects.
Marijuana Use Is Rising Across the United States
"Previous research has indicated that cannabis use is rapidly increasing in the United States, with 1 in 6 adults in 2024 reporting having used it within the last month, up from 1 in 10 in 2020 -- a 51% increase," said study author Aabha Divya, M.B.B.S., M.Ch., an assistant professor in the division of cardiothoracic surgery at the Tulane University School of Medicine in New Orleans.
Earlier research conducted between 2016 and 2020 had already identified associations between cannabis consumption and unfavorable cardiovascular outcomes. Those findings also suggested that using cannabis more frequently during a given month was connected to greater cardiovascular risk.
However, the evidence has not always been consistent. With recreational marijuana becoming legal in more places and cannabis products increasingly available, Divya and colleagues wanted to investigate these possible health effects in a larger population.
"We wanted to expand on this earlier work because cannabis use has become increasingly common in the United States, as recreational legalization and commercial availability of various products with cannabis have also expanded. Previous studies have raised concerns about possible cardiovascular effects; however, the results have not been consistent," Divya said.
The researchers examined information collected through the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), a large telephone survey of American adults. They combined responses from jurisdictions that collected information about cannabis consumption between 2020 and 2024.
Participants answered questions about their marijuana use and whether a healthcare professional had ever diagnosed them with cardiovascular conditions, including a heart attack, stroke, or coronary heart disease.
Even Occasional Marijuana Use Was Linked to Higher Stroke Odds
One of the most striking findings was that infrequent cannabis use was associated with cardiovascular problems. In fact, the researchers did not find the steady increase in cardiovascular risk with more frequent use that they had expected.
The analysis revealed several important associations:
- Occasional cannabis use: Adults who reported using cannabis on 1 to 5 days per month had 23% higher odds of reporting a history of cardiovascular disease compared with those who reported no use.
- Heavy cannabis use: People who consumed cannabis on 16 to 30 days per month had 21% higher odds of reporting a history of cardiovascular disease.
- Stroke: The strongest association involved stroke. People reporting low-frequency cannabis use had 40% higher odds of reporting a history of stroke, while heavy users had 25% higher odds.
- Heart attacks: Researchers found no statistically significant association between how frequently participants used cannabis and whether they had experienced a heart attack.
These findings were unexpected because the relationship between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease did not consistently become stronger as consumption increased.
"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward. We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease," Divya said.
Although the study cannot establish that marijuana directly causes strokes or other cardiovascular conditions, the findings suggest that occasional consumption should not automatically be considered free of potential cardiovascular concerns.
"As cannabis use becomes more common, it is increasingly important that people and their healthcare professionals include it in conversations about cardiovascular health, just as they discuss tobacco, alcohol and other commonly used substances," she added.
Experts Urge Greater Attention to Cannabis and Heart Health
Robert L. Page II, Pharm.D., M.S.P.H., FAHA, who led the writing group responsible for the American Heart Association's 2020 cannabis scientific statement, said the findings add to growing concerns about marijuana's possible cardiovascular effects.
One challenge in evaluating those effects is that many cannabis users also smoke tobacco. Because tobacco is already an established cardiovascular risk factor, separating its effects from those of cannabis can be difficult.
Page, who was not involved in the research, explained why the new findings deserve attention.
"Unfortunately, many patients who use cannabis may also smoke tobacco, which completely clouds the issue when addressing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk. In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case. This is the second observational study to suggest that cannabis exposure (without tobacco smoking) may be a potential risk factor for developing cardiovascular disease. Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events. To this end, clinicians should be addressing cannabis use with their patients as they would tobacco use when considering the risk of cardiovascular disease."
Page is a professor in the department of clinical pharmacy and the department of physical medicine/rehabilitation at the University of Colorado Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences in Aurora, Colorado.
How Researchers Studied Nearly Half a Million Americans
The analysis included 442,906 adults living in the United States (average age of 49 years; approximately half women). Their responses came from telephone surveys conducted through the BRFSS.
Researchers used survey information collected from 2020 through 2024, focusing on states that had included an optional marijuana questionnaire. Between 16 and 24 states participated in this portion of the survey each year, meaning the analysis did not represent every state.
Participants reported how many days they had consumed cannabis during the preceding month. The questions covered multiple ways of using marijuana (smoking, vaping or ingesting gummies or other cannabis-containing foods).
The researchers divided participants into four categories based on their reported use:
- No recent use: No cannabis consumption during the previous 30 days.
- Low-frequency use: Cannabis consumption on 1 to 5 days during the previous month.
- Moderate-frequency use: Consumption on 6 to 15 days.
- Heavy use: Consumption on 16 to 30 days.
Participants also indicated whether they had ever received a diagnosis of heart attack, heart disease, heart-related chest pain, or stroke.
To better distinguish the association with cannabis from other potential explanations, the researchers accounted for numerous established cardiovascular risk factors. These included demographic characteristics, tobacco smoking, alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, physical inactivity, education, and income.
Why the Findings Do Not Prove Marijuana Causes Strokes
Despite the large number of participants, the study has several limitations that affect how its findings should be interpreted.
First, the analysis examined associations between reported cannabis use and previously diagnosed cardiovascular conditions at a single point in time. This means researchers could not determine whether marijuana use preceded the cardiovascular problems or whether it directly contributed to them.
The information also depended on participants accurately recalling and reporting their cannabis consumption and medical histories (making them subject to potential errors in memory). Such reports may not always reflect actual patterns of use or diagnoses.
Another limitation was the lack of information about the strength of the cannabis products participants consumed or the quantities they used. Without those details, the researchers could not evaluate whether THC potency or the amount consumed influenced the observed associations.
The researchers also acknowledged that some participants may have reduced or discontinued cannabis consumption after being diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. As a result, the group reporting no cannabis use in the previous month may have included former users.
These uncertainties make it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how consumption frequency affects cardiovascular health. Nevertheless, the findings add to growing evidence that cannabis use deserves closer examination as a possible factor in heart disease and stroke.
As marijuana becomes more widely available and its use continues to increase, researchers and healthcare professionals are emphasizing the importance of discussing cannabis alongside other substances that may affect cardiovascular health.

articles.title: Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't
articles.text:
Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't
- Date:
- November 10, 2026
- Source:
- Florida International University
- Summary:
- A surprising new study reveals that mosquitoes have very different tastes in humans, with each species attracted to its own combination of skin odors, chemicals, and bacteria. The discovery challenges the idea of a universal mosquito magnet and could lead to more effective repellents against dangerous disease-spreading mosquitoes.
- Share:
Some people seem to attract mosquitoes wherever they go, but new research reveals that being a mosquito magnet depends on which species is doing the biting.
In a study published in iScience, researchers at Florida International University (FIU) tested how three of the world's most dangerous mosquito species responded to 119 human volunteers. Surprisingly, not a single participant attracted all three species. Instead, each species favored a different group of people, largely based on their individual body chemistry and natural skin odors.
The discovery could change how scientists approach the prevention of mosquito-borne diseases. Because different mosquito species respond to different chemical signals from human skin, researchers may eventually be able to create next-generation, species-specific repellents that offer more targeted protection.
"Isolating the components of human odor that attract or repel mosquitoes could lead to novel strategies to combat vector-borne diseases," said Matthew DeGennaro, a neurogeneticist who leads the research team and directs the Biomolecular Sciences Institute at FIU, Miami's state university.
Different Mosquito Species Prefer Different People
The researchers investigated three species responsible for spreading serious illnesses, including yellow fever, dengue, Zika, West Nile and other diseases. These were Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito) and Culex quinquefasciatus (southern house mosquito).
Led by Ph.D. student Kaylee Marrero, the investigation was the first to directly compare how several mosquito species reacted to the same human participants. The findings revealed unexpected differences in the chemical and microbial signals each species appeared to use when choosing whom to bite.
"We didn't expect the species to prefer different people when we started the study," Marrero said. "Each species having a distinct microbial signature that they use as a cue was so surprising to me."
Each mosquito species showed its own distinct preferences:
- Aedes aegypti: This species favored people who were not wearing added fragrances and whose skin contained lower levels of certain volatile chemical compounds. It typically bites during the day and showed a slight preference for men over women.
- Aedes albopictus: Also known as the Asian tiger mosquito, this daytime feeder was particularly attracted to people whose skin released higher levels of ketones and naturally occurring plant-like volatile compounds.
- Culex quinquefasciatus: Unlike the other two species, the southern house mosquito feeds after dark and appeared especially sensitive to the skin microbiome, the community of bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms that naturally inhabit human skin. Certain bacterial families made people more attractive, while others seemed to discourage the mosquitoes from biting.
The Hidden Chemistry Behind Mosquito Attraction
Human body odor is far more complicated than it might seem. Our skin releases a mixture of more than 1,000 volatile organic compounds, many of which scientists have yet to fully identify or understand.
The researchers found that the three mosquito species did not share a common preference for particular individuals. Instead, each consistently favored its own subset of volunteers, suggesting that different species have evolved distinct methods for detecting and interpreting human scent.
To investigate what made certain people more appealing, the team collected samples of participants' body odors and skin microbiomes alongside the mosquito preference tests. They then examined which chemical compounds and microorganisms were present and measured their relative abundance.
The results showed strong connections between the mosquitoes' preferences and differences in the chemical and microbial makeup of people's skin.
"This connected so well with the differences in skin bacteria and odors," DeGennaro said. "It is clear to me now that our skin microbiomes define our human odor signature. Each species found its own way to decode that signature."
Could This Discovery Lead to Better Mosquito Repellents?
Understanding why one mosquito species finds a person attractive while another does not could open new possibilities for preventing dangerous infections.
By identifying the specific chemical compounds and skin bacteria that attract or discourage different mosquitoes, the FIU researchers are helping establish a scientific foundation for more precisely targeted repellents.
The findings could also improve public health strategies by allowing communities to focus on the particular mosquito species responsible for spreading disease in their region.
Rather than assuming that all mosquitoes are drawn to the same people for the same reasons, future prevention methods may be designed around the distinct chemical preferences of each species.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Florida International University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Kaylee M. Marrero, John S. Castillo, Dani Lucas-Barbosa, Anthony J. Bellantuono, Matthew A. Marrero, Dariel Cid, Andre L. Costa-da-Silva, Niels O. Verhulst, Matthew DeGennaro. Individual humans are more attractive to certain mosquito species. iScience, 2026; 29 (8): 117006 DOI: 10.1016/j.isci.2026.117006

articles.title: Sự khác biệt về con rồng giữa phương Đông và phương Tây
articles.text:
Dù là loài vật chỉ có trong truyền thuyết, nhưng con rồng trong con mắt của người phương Tây và phương Đông có sự khác biệt rất lớn.
Theo thông tin từ trang web Draconika.com, loài rồng ở phương Tây thường được coi là biểu tượng của sự xấu xa, khi loài vật này có thể bay và phun ra lửa. Nhiều truyền thuyết phương Tây thường miêu tả rồng là một loài vật xảo trá, thường canh giữ các kho báu hoặc được sử dụng để làm mục tiêu chinh phục của các vị anh hùng.
Tượng con rồng phương Tây ở Đại học Drexel, Mỹ. (Ảnh: Wikipedia).
Hình tượng con rồng ở phương Tây đôi khi được sử dụng làm biểu tượng chiến tranh hoặc bảo hộ. Người Viking sinh sống ở khu vực Bắc Âu thường sử dụng một loại thuyền có tên drakkar để chở các chiến binh của họ đi chinh phạt nhiều khu vực ở châu Âu. Một số con tàu cũng được trang bị một bức điêu khắc hình đầu rồng ở khu vực mũi tàu, nhằm xua đuổi những linh hồn tà ác hay rắn biển mỗi khi thực hiện chuyến đi biển.
Hình vẽ về con thuyền drakkar. (Ảnh: Wikipedia).
Trong thần thoại Hy Lạp, loài rồng cũng từng xuất hiện trong một số câu chuyện liên quan tới thần mặt trời Apollo và thần cai quản bầu trời Zeus với vai trò như một nhân vật phản diện. Hay trong câu chuyện “Jason và đoàn thám hiểm Argonauts”, những người anh hùng buộc phải chiến đấu với một con rồng để giành được vật báu là bộ lông cừu vàng (The Golden Fleece).
Ở Pháp, người dân nước này thường truyền tai nhau về một câu chuyện có tên “Thánh Martha và con rồng”. Nội dung chuyện này kể về một con rồng tên là Tarasque hoành hành ở thị trấn Nerluc nằm gần sông Rhone vào giữa thế kỷ thứ 1 sau Công nguyên. Dù người dân ở đây đã tìm đủ cách để tiêu diệt con rồng, nhưng đều vô dụng trước sức mạnh của Tarasque.
Thánh Martha và con rồng. (Ảnh: Wikipedia).
Về sau, người dân thị trấn Nerluc phải mời một nữ tu có tên Martha tới để bắt con rồng. Với sức mạnh của mình, Martha đã nhanh chóng thu phục được con quái vật. Người dân thị trấn Nerluc, để ghi nhớ công lao của nữ tu Martha, đã đổi tên thị trấn này thành Tarascon (nay thuộc tỉnh Bouches-du-Rhone, Pháp).
Tuy nhiên, câu chuyện nổi tiếng của phương Tây có liên quan tới loại rồng lại liên quan tới truyền thuyết Beowulf. Nội dung câu chuyện xoay quanh việc một con rồng do tức giận vì kho báu của nó bị trộm nên đã tới tàn phá vương quốc Geat, nơi vua Beowulf trị vì. Vua Beowulf, dù đã tuổi già sức yếu, nhưng vẫn quyết tâm đối đầu con quái vật. Dù đã tiêu diệt được con rồng, nhưng Beowulf cũng tử trận do nhiều vết thương từ quái thú.
Trái ngược với hình tượng xấu trong quan niệm của người phương Tây, con rồng của người phương Đông, nhất là với người dân Trung Quốc, là sinh vật nhân từ và đáng được tôn kính. Riêng với các bậc vua chúa, rồng chính là biểu tượng của quyền lực, bởi người đứng đầu thiên hạ phải là người có trí tuệ siêu phàm.
Điêu khắc hình rồng tại một danh thắng ở tỉnh Thiểm Tây, Trung Quốc. (Ảnh: Wikipedia).
Họa gia Đổng Vũ sống dưới thời Ngũ đại Thập quốc (907-979) trong lịch sử Trung Quốc từng miêu tả con rồng là sự kết hợp từ đặc trưng của những loài động vật như “sừng của hươu; đầu của bò; mắt giống loài tôm; miệng lạc đà; bụng của rắn; vảy của cá; chân của chim phượng; có ria; tai của voi”.
Theo trang History skills, sự kết hợp từ tất cả đặc điểm của những loài vật trên cho thấy rồng là biểu tượng của sức mạnh và thế giới tự nhiên. Sức mạnh của con rồng phương Đông được mô tả có thể hô mưa, gọi gió, điều khiển các nguyên tố... gây tác động đến thế giới tự nhiên, thời tiết và mùa màng. Không chỉ vậy, con rồng còn là biểu tượng cho trí tuệ và sự thông thái. Hình dáng dài của rồng hay đi kèm với một viên ngọc, đại diện cho trí tuệ, sự khai sáng.
Ngoài ra, con rồng cũng tượng trưng cho sự biến đổi. Chẳng hạn, rồng có khả năng bay lượn giữa trời và đất, thay đổi kích thước... Điều này phản ánh cuộc sống của con người biến đổi không ngừng.

articles.title: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
articles.text:
Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
- Date:
- November 10, 2026
- Source:
- McGill University
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.
- Share:
An ancient rodent of extraordinary size has been identified from fossils uncovered in a mine in southern Thailand. The discovery, made by an international team of paleontologists that includes scientists from McGill University, provides new evidence that giant rodents appeared much earlier and in more parts of the world than previously believed.
The researchers found "remarkably large" fossilized teeth belonging to a previously unknown species called Yakamys sirindhornae. This prehistoric rodent lived approximately 34 million years ago, during the middle of the Paleogene period. Its remains, consisting of a lower second molar and a lower incisor, were recovered from the Bang Mark Pit at the Krabi lignite mine in Thailand's Krabi Province.
Although only two teeth have been identified, they offer valuable clues about rodent gigantism, the evolutionary process through which rodents develop unusually large bodies. The discovery suggests that Southeast Asia played a more significant role in the early evolution of giant rodents than scientists had recognized.
Giant Rodents Have a Much Older History Than Expected
"Today, the largest living rodent is the capybara, but very large rodents are not restricted to recent ecosystems," said Virginie Millien, a biology professor at McGill University and co-author of the study. "Giant rodents evolved repeatedly during the later history of the group, mostly in South America. This discovery suggests that Southeast Asia also played an important role in the early evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents."
The newly identified animal's name reflects both its impressive size and its connection to Thailand. Yakamys combines "yak," the Thai word for giant, with "mys," the Greek word for mouse or rat.
The second part of its scientific name recognizes an important supporter of scientific research in Thailand.
"The species name, sirindhornae, honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, in recognition of her longstanding support for science and paleontological research in Thailand," Millien said.
How Big Was This 34-Million-Year-Old Rodent?
To estimate the animal's size, the research team applied seven established methods that use tooth measurements to calculate body mass. Their results suggest that Yakamys sirindhornae weighed approximately 30 kilograms, making it about twice as heavy as other known rodents from the same period, including Hulgana.
That would have made the newly discovered species exceptionally large compared with its contemporaries. However, the researchers emphasize that determining an extinct animal's weight from a small number of fossilized teeth involves considerable uncertainty.
"This is only a ballpark figure, as there is substantial uncertainty associated with fossil body-mass estimation," Millien said.
The limited fossil evidence also makes it difficult to reconstruct how Yakamys evolved or what its life was like. Additional discoveries will be needed to better understand its physical characteristics, ecological role, and evolutionary relationships.
International Research Uncovers Thailand's Prehistoric Past
The fossils were identified through an ongoing international collaboration investigating ancient mammals in Thailand's Krabi Basin. The project brings together scientists from McGill University, Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources, and French research organizations, including CNRS and Université de Poitiers.
By revealing evidence of an unusually large rodent in Southeast Asia 34 million years ago, the discovery expands scientists' understanding of where and when rodent gigantism emerged. Future fossil finds could help establish how these ancient giants lived and how their evolution relates to the enormous rodents that appeared elsewhere in the world.
The research received support from CNRS, Université de Poitiers, Université de Montpellier, McGill University, and the Department of Mineral Resources of Thailand.

articles.title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
articles.text:
237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
- Date:
- November 10, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Davis
- Summary:
- A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater. Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.
- Share:
A remarkable fossil discovery in China has revealed an ancient amphibian that lived entirely in the ocean, something no amphibian alive today is known to do. The unusual animal, named Gerrothorax maritimus, had a broad, flattened body protected by bony armor and was roughly the size of a giant salamander. Researchers believe it spent much of its life on the seafloor, waiting to ambush passing prey.
The discovery comes from an international team at the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. Their findings, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, are based on two exceptionally well-preserved skeletons dating back nearly 237 million years to the Late Triassic period.
Both fossils were uncovered in China's Guizhou Province, in a region that was once submerged beneath an ancient ocean hundreds of miles from major landmasses.
"This area is part of an ecosystem that we've been looking at and trying to reconstruct," said study corresponding author Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UC Davis. "We've been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian, and it's a sort of very unusual member of the lineage."
The finding is especially surprising because amphibians are generally unable to survive in seawater. Among the more than 8,000 amphibian species living today, none are known to spend their entire lives in marine environments, and fewer than 2% have any ability to tolerate salt.
Mammals, reptiles, and birds, by comparison, all include species that can live entirely at sea without relying on land for food or fresh water. Until this discovery, scientists had never identified convincing fossil evidence of an amphibian with the same ability.
A Giant Armored Amphibian Built for the Seafloor
Because the two skeletons are so complete, researchers were able to piece together the animal's appearance and develop a clearer picture of how it lived.
Gerrothorax maritimus measured nearly three feet long, but its proportions were far different from those of a modern salamander. Rather than having a long, slender body, it was unusually broad and flattened, with a distinctive disc-shaped form.
Its body was also covered in thick bony armor, which may have helped protect it from large marine predators such as ichthyosaurs.
"If you think about today's amphibians, this animal is unusual because it's big," Motani said. "It's probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what's different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky."
The structure of its skull, together with its heavy armor, suggests that this ancient amphibian was an ambush predator. Instead of actively chasing its meals, it likely rested on the seafloor until an unsuspecting animal came within reach.
"They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in," said Motani, who noted that the hunting strategy resembles that of the wobbegong, a type of carpet shark that lives near the seafloor and captures prey using suction.
How Could an Amphibian Survive in Salt Water?
One of the biggest mysteries surrounding Gerrothorax maritimus is how it managed to survive in an environment that is hostile to nearly all modern amphibians.
The problem comes down largely to amphibian skin. Unlike the relatively waterproof skin of many other animals, amphibian skin allows water and gases to pass through it. This makes it useful for breathing and maintaining hydration, but also leaves amphibians especially vulnerable to the effects of salt water.
"That skin is permeable, and that allows the animals to use it for multiple purposes," said Motani. "They use it for respiration and water intake, so amphibians don't drink or breathe through the mouth because they can do both through the skin."
As a result, modern amphibians generally depend on freshwater habitats or environments close to them. A few species have developed limited salt tolerance, including the crab-eating frog. Even these animals can lose weight when exposed to brackish water and must eventually return to freshwater to recover.
The ancient Gerrothorax maritimus, however, may have evolved a very different solution.
Researchers suggest that its extensive bony armor restricted the movement of water through its skin. This protective covering may have reduced its dependence on absorbing water directly through the skin, allowing the animal to take in seawater through its mouth instead.
Under this proposed mechanism, water would have been absorbed through the digestive tract, while the animal's gills could have helped eliminate excess salt. Gills are known to have been present in members of the Gerrothorax genus, giving the researchers reason to suspect that this species possessed a more fishlike approach to managing its salt balance.
Together, these adaptations may explain how an amphibian managed to occupy an ecological niche that remains inaccessible to its modern relatives.
Fossil Evidence Points to a Fully Marine Lifestyle
The researchers also examined whether Gerrothorax maritimus truly lived in the ocean or whether its remains might have been transported there after death.
Several clues strongly favor a marine lifestyle.
First, the skeletons were recovered from sediments deposited in a deep marine environment. Their remarkable completeness also provides important evidence about where the animals died.
"Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom," said Motani. "But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived."
The preservation of such delicate skeletal structures suggests that the bodies were not carried long distances before reaching the seafloor.
To investigate further, the team analyzed the fossils' chemical composition, focusing on the relative abundance of different forms of strontium, known as isotopes.
The results closely matched the strontium isotope signatures expected in ocean water during the Late Triassic, providing another independent line of evidence that the animals inhabited a marine environment.
Taken together, the fossil preservation, geological setting, and chemical findings make a compelling case that Gerrothorax maritimus spent its life entirely at sea.
The discovery reveals an unexpected evolutionary path for amphibians, showing that at least one ancient species appears to have overcome the biological limitations that keep its living relatives largely confined to freshwater environments.
The research received funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

Materials provided by University of California - Davis. Original written by Greg Watry. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
