articles.title: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
articles.text:
Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
- Date:
- November 9, 2026
- Source:
- The University of Hong Kong
- Summary:
- A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults suggests that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The surprising findings raise the possibility that medications already used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain.
- Share:
A common class of drugs used to treat osteoporosis may have an unexpected benefit: lowering the risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. In a study involving more than 120,000 older adults, researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed) found that patients taking certain medications to strengthen their bones were significantly less likely to develop dementia.
The medications, known as nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NBPs), are widely prescribed to prevent bone loss and fractures. The findings suggest that these established treatments could potentially serve a second purpose by helping protect the aging brain. The research, conducted by scientists in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed's LKS Faculty of Medicine, was published in Alzheimer's & Dementia.
More than 55 million people worldwide currently live with dementia, and that number is projected to climb to 139 million by 2050. The World Health Organization has identified dementia as a major global health priority. Although the first medications designed to slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) have recently gained approval, their high costs, limited suitability for some patients, and questions about their effectiveness remain important challenges.
These obstacles have increased interest in finding affordable ways to prevent or delay dementia before symptoms develop. One promising approach is to identify existing medications that might offer benefits beyond the conditions they were originally designed to treat.
The Surprising Connection Between Bone Health and Dementia
Osteoporosis and dementia often affect the same older adults. Osteoporosis causes bones to become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures, while dementia progressively affects memory, thinking, and the ability to carry out everyday activities. The two conditions also share several risk factors, including older age, being female, and low levels of physical activity.
Previous research by the same HKUMed team established that osteoporosis and fractures are independent risk factors for dementia. The researchers also found that people already living with dementia face an increased likelihood of falling and breaking bones.
This relationship raises an intriguing possibility: medications that treat osteoporosis might also help reduce dementia risk.
Among the most commonly prescribed osteoporosis treatments are alendronate and zoledronate, both of which belong to the NBP drug class. These medications work by slowing the breakdown of bone tissue, helping maintain bone strength and reduce the likelihood of fractures.
Scientists have also begun uncovering evidence that some of the biological processes influenced by these drugs may be involved in the development of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. This overlap has prompted researchers to investigate whether NBPs might provide benefits for the brain as well as the skeleton.
Study of 120,000 Patients Finds Up to 24% Lower Dementia Risk
To explore this possibility, the HKUMed researchers examined electronic medical records from across Hong Kong, analyzing data from more than 120,000 patients aged 60 and older. All participants had osteoporosis or fragility fractures, which are breaks that can occur after relatively minor injuries because the bones have become weakened.
The records covered the period from 2005 through 2020, allowing the team to investigate how different osteoporosis treatments were associated with dementia risk over time.
The results revealed a notable difference. Patients taking NBPs had a 16% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias compared with patients who received no osteoporosis medication.
The association was even stronger when NBP users were compared with patients taking other types of osteoporosis drugs. In that comparison, dementia risk was 24% lower among those receiving NBPs.
Women and patients who had experienced hip fractures appeared to show particularly strong associations between NBP treatment and reduced dementia risk.
The researchers also estimated that treating 48 patients with NBPs over five years could potentially prevent one case of dementia. If future research confirms that the medications directly reduce dementia risk, the implications could be substantial, particularly for older adults who already need treatment for osteoporosis.
Because the findings come from an observational study, they do not establish that the drugs themselves prevent dementia. However, they provide evidence supporting further investigation into whether these medications could help delay or prevent cognitive decline.
Could Existing Osteoporosis Drugs Help Prevent Alzheimer's?
Professor Cheung Ching-lung, Associate Professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed, believes the findings highlight the possibility that a familiar osteoporosis treatment could deliver two important health benefits.
"Our study provides evidence that NBPs may offer dual benefits in strengthening bones and reducing fracture risk, as well as potentially preventing ADRD. Their potential neuroprotective role provides an empirical basis and supports future research on the actual effectiveness of this medication in preventing or delaying cognitive decline associated with ADRD."
The potential advantage of this approach is that NBPs are already widely available and have an established history of use in treating osteoporosis. Rather than developing an entirely new medication from scratch, researchers could investigate whether these existing treatments offer additional protection for people at elevated risk of dementia.
The findings are particularly relevant as populations around the world grow older and the number of people affected by dementia continues to rise.
"These findings are significant as they demonstrate a potential approach for reducing dementia risk in a vulnerable population using safe and widely available NBPs. In our rapidly aging society, these findings suggest that while waiting for the novel therapies, existing medications can also provide additional protection for high-risk populations," said Professor Cheung.
Further studies will be needed to determine whether NBPs can directly prevent or delay Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Nevertheless, the results suggest that medications already prescribed to protect aging bones may also have an important role to play in protecting brain health.
About the Research Team
The research was led by Professor Cheung Ching-lung of the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed. Dr Sing Chor-wing, from the same department, served as the study's first author.
Additional researchers included Professor Chan Koon-ho, Dr Patrick Chiu Ka-chun, and Professor Kathryn Tan Choon-beng, all from the Department of Medicine in the School of Clinical Medicine at HKUMed.

Journal Reference:

Bisphosphonates and the risk of dementia in patients with osteoporosis or fragility fracture: A population‐based study in Hong Kong. Alzheimer\'s, 2025; 21 (7) DOI: 10.1002/alz.70503

articles.title: Satellite snaps rare birds-eye view of the ISS | Space photo of the day for Nov. 12, 2026
articles.text:
Satellite snaps rare birds-eye view of the ISS | Space photo of the day for Nov. 12, 2026
Here's something you don't see every day.
A commercial satellite has spotted the International Space Station (ISS), giving us a unique view of the orbiting lab from above.
What is it?
Most of the time, when we see the ISS, it is from down here on Earth or from the viewpoint of the astronauts onboard, peering out the windows at the station's limbs, solar arrays and instruments.
But in this snapshot, which was posted on X on Nov. 9 by the Australian company HEO, we can see the station stretched out in all its glory.
HEO specializes in using satellites in low Earth orbit to capture images of other spacecraft, though longer-term the company aims to capture observations far out into the solar system. HEO doesn't build the satellites that take these photos; rather, the company's software tasks the spacecraft to image targets as they come into range.
This great photo of the ISS from above, for example, was taken by a satellite operated by BlackSky, a Virginia-based company that holds a non-Earth imaging agreement with HEO.
So far, HEO and its partners have captured imagery of a variety of spacecraft in orbit, including the ISS, China's Tiangong space station and the European Space Agency's ERS-2 satellite (while it was hurtling back to Earth in 2024).
Why is it incredible?
While it might seem that satellites are just hovering above Earth, the space station and other spacecraft in LEO are hurtling through space at roughly 17,500 mph (28,160 kph), hundreds of miles above our planet's surface.
A snapshot of a satellite from above is therefore far from mundane. Rather, it requires incredible coordination and technical skill; satellite operators must know precisely when their target will present itself, and their equipment must be capable of getting the shot.
Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music

articles.title: Chinese scientists cool atoms to coldest temperatures ever observed in record-breaking space station experiment
articles.text:
Chinese scientists cool atoms to near absolute zero in record-breaking space experiment
Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.
Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.
Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.
Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.
The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.
The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.
"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.
How low can you go?
Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.
The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.
That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.
Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.

Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space. Science, eaea5324. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aea5324
Elizabeth Howell was staff reporter at Space.com between 2022 and 2024 and a regular contributor to Live Science and Space.com between 2012 and 2022. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, speaking several times with the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

articles.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
articles.text:
DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
- Date:
- November 8, 2026
- Source:
- University of Lancashire
- Summary:
- The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered a remarkable collection of DNA hidden within the Shroud of Turin, revealing a surprisingly complex biological history behind one of the world's most mysterious and controversial religious artifacts. The genetic evidence includes traces of humans, bacteria, fungi, plants, animals, and even Mediterranean red coral, offering new clues about the environments and people that have come into contact with the famous cloth over the centuries.
Published in Scientific Reports, the study used advanced DNA sequencing technology to examine samples collected from the Shroud in 1978. For the first time, researchers applied a sophisticated technique (rigorous PCR-free next-generation metagenomic sequencing) to these officially collected samples, allowing them to identify genetic material preserved within the linen fibers in unprecedented detail.
Unlike traditional DNA testing, which often focuses on genetic material from a single organism, metagenomic sequencing can detect DNA from many different species within the same sample. This makes it particularly useful for studying historical objects that have been handled, stored, and exposed to changing environments over long periods.
By examining this genetic material, the international research team assembled what they describe as the most comprehensive picture yet of the biological traces accumulated on the Shroud throughout its history.
Human DNA and a Hidden World of Microorganisms
Among the discoveries were multiple lineages of human mitochondrial DNA, suggesting that genetic material from different human populations has accumulated on the cloth. Mitochondrial DNA is a small portion of our genetic material that is inherited through the maternal line, making it especially useful for studying ancestry and population history.
The researchers also identified an unexpectedly diverse microbiome, the collection of microscopic organisms associated with a particular environment or object. These included bacteria commonly found on human skin, various fungi, and microorganisms adapted to living in salty environments.
Some of these organisms belong to a group known as archaea, which are single-celled microorganisms distinct from bacteria. Certain archaea can thrive in extremely salty conditions that would be difficult for many other forms of life to tolerate.
Together, these findings reveal that the Shroud carries a complicated biological record shaped by repeated human contact and exposure to different environmental conditions.
DNA From Plants, Animals, and Mediterranean Coral
The discoveries extended far beyond human DNA and microorganisms. Scientists also detected genetic traces from numerous plant and animal species, adding another layer to the Shroud's biological history.
Plant DNA included cultivated wheat, carrots, maize, bananas, and peanuts. Genetic material from domesticated animals was also present, including cattle, pigs, chickens, dogs, and cats.
One particularly unusual finding was DNA associated with Mediterranean red coral.
The wide variety of biological material suggests that the cloth has encountered a diverse range of living organisms and environmental influences. These genetic traces may reflect its long history of handling, storage, and movement through different geographical regions.
Importantly, the presence of DNA from a particular species does not establish when that material reached the cloth. Some traces could have accumulated relatively recently, while others may reflect much older interactions. This makes the findings valuable for reconstructing the Shroud's environmental history, but also highlights the difficulty of interpreting DNA recovered from an object that has been exposed to human activity for centuries.
Can DNA Solve the Mystery of the Shroud of Turin?
Despite the remarkable diversity of genetic material, the researchers emphasize that their findings cannot establish the Shroud's age or authenticity.
The Shroud of Turin is a linen cloth bearing the faint image of a human figure and has long been associated by some believers with the burial of Jesus. Its origins have been debated for generations, making it one of the most extensively investigated historical and religious artifacts in the world.
Because the cloth has been touched and exposed to different environments over many centuries, its DNA represents a mixture of biological material accumulated at different times. This makes it impossible to reliably separate any original DNA that might have been associated with the fabric from the many genetic traces deposited afterward.
Instead, the research demonstrates how modern forensic genomics and proteomics can reveal information that traditional methods might miss. Forensic genomics uses genetic evidence to investigate biological origins and interactions, while proteomics examines proteins, which can also preserve valuable clues about biological materials.
Together, these approaches offer powerful new ways to investigate how historical objects have been preserved, handled, and exposed to different environments.
Modern DNA Technology Reveals New Historical Clues
Professor Noemi Procopio, Professor of Forensic Science at the University of Lancashire, contributed to the international research collaboration. She emphasized that advances in forensic technology are making it possible to recover information from historical samples collected decades earlier.
Professor Noemi Procopio, Professor of Forensic Science at the University of Lancashire, said: "The Shroud of Turin continues to fascinate historians, scientists and the public, and we're thrilled to reveal new information about the biological complexity preserved within samples collected almost 50 years ago by applying new cutting-edge forensic DNA technologies.
"The Shroud represents a rich archive of genetic information that has accumulated over centuries of human interaction and environmental exposure. While the DNA evidence cannot answer all the questions about the age or authenticity of the cloth, it provides novel insights into its biological history and demonstrates how advances in forensic science can unlock new information from historical artifacts."

Perego, Massimo Iorizzo, Timothy F. Sharbel, Pierluigi Baima Bollone, Antonio Torroni, Andrea Squartini, Alessandro Achilli. DNA signatures preserved in the official 1978 sample collection of the Shroud of Turin. Scientific Reports, 2026; 16 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-60684-7

articles.title: The 'eclipse of the century' will plunge these 8 wonders of the Roman Empire into darkness on Aug. 2, 2027
articles.text:
The 'eclipse of the century' will plunge these 8 wonders of the Roman Empire into darkness on Aug. 2, 2027
Ancient Roman cities, temples and amphitheaters across the Mediterranean will fall into the moon's shadow during the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027.
Ancient Egyptian temples will inevitably dominate the story of the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027.
After all, the path of totality crosses Luxor, home to Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the ancient world's most famous monuments. But follow the moon's shadow west and another ancient civilization comes into view. Before reaching Egypt, totality will sweep across the Mediterranean and North Africa, passing over an extraordinary collection of Roman cities, fortresses, theaters, temples and triumphal arches. Many lie within what became Rome's North African provinces, a region that produced some of the empire's wealthiest and most impressive cities.
From beachside Baelo Claudia in Spain and military Tamuda in Morocco to Timgad and Djémila in Algeria and the jaw-dropping El Jem Amphitheater in Tunisia, Roman ruins will experience between two and more than five minutes of darkness — creating extraordinary possibilities for eclipse chasers and photographers. Here are some of the best places to watch the moon's shadow cross what was once the Roman Empire. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.
1. Baelo Claudia, Spain
Location: near Tarifa, Andalucía, Spain
Start of totality and duration: 10:44 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 31 seconds
Historical cloud cover: 12%
Altitude of the sun: 37 degrees above east
Roman ruins, an Atlantic beach and the mountains of Africa could all share the frame with the eclipsed sun at Baelo Claudia. Founded in the second century B.C., this remarkably well-preserved Roman city near Bolonia beach includes a forum, basilica, theater, temples, baths and a decumanus maximus (east-west street), all set against forested hills and a vast coastal sand dune. For photographers, the possibilities are exceptional — columns and temples may provide an ancient foreground, while wider compositions could incorporate the beach and dunes. On particularly clear days, Morocco is visible across the Strait of Gibraltar — potentially putting Roman ruins, two continents and a total solar eclipse into one extraordinary scene.
2. Málaga Roman Theatre, Spain
Location: Málaga, Spain
Start of totality and duration: 10:48 a.m. CEST; 1 minute, 57 seconds
Historical cloud cover: 9%
Altitude of the sun: 39 degrees above east
Few eclipse locations can offer two civilizations in the same photograph. Málaga's Roman Theatre was built in the first century B.C., when the city was part of the Roman province of Hispania, and today sits directly beneath the Alcazaba, the imposing Muslim-era palace-fortress that dominates the hillside above. Although its totality is considerably shorter than locations farther south, the photographic possibilities are compelling. From a carefully chosen position, it may be possible to frame the darkened sun with the theater's ancient stonework and the walls of the Alcazaba rising behind it. Another major advantage for eclipse chasers is that this extraordinary historical setting sits in the heart of Málaga, making it one of the most accessible ancient sites on the path of totality.
3. Tamuda, Morocco
Location: Tétouan, Morocco
Start of totality and duration: 08:45 a.m. GMT; 4 minutes, 51 seconds
Historical cloud cover: 14%
Altitude of sun: 38 degrees above east-southeast
Long before the Romans arrived in northern Morocco, Tamuda was already a thriving Mauretanian settlement. Founded around the third century B.C. in the Martil Valley, near modern Tétouan, the Romans established a fortified military camp here in the first century A.D., whose massive stone walls remain the defining feature of this archaeological site. Tamuda combines long totality, promising weather and an atmospheric archaeological foreground — yet remains far less famous than the Roman sites across the Strait of Gibraltar.
4. Timgad, Algeria
Location: near Batna, Algeria
Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds
Historical cloud cover: 5%
Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast
Few places in the 2027 path of totality combine ancient architecture and long totality quite like Timgad. Founded around A.D. 100 as the Roman colony of Thamugadi, this remarkably well-preserved city sits on an open plateau at the foot of Algeria's Aurès Mountains. Its grid of streets, forum, theater, temples, baths and columns survives alongside its most famous monument, the three-arched gateway traditionally known as the Arch of Trajan. A relatively high sun will make close architectural compositions challenging, but Timgad's wide-open site provides plenty of possibilities for carefully planned wide-angle images.
5. Lambaesis, Algeria
Location: near Batna, Algeria
Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds
Historical cloud cover: 5%
Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast
Just 12—15 miles (20—25 km) west of Timgad lies its military counterpart. Lambaesis was the principal base of Rome's Legio III Augusta, the legion that helped secure Rome's African Empire. Rather than an entire gridded colonial city, the attraction here is monumental military architecture, most notably the imposing remains of the heart of the fortress. The eclipse circumstances are almost identical to nearby Timgad, with more than five minutes of totality and historically excellent prospects for clear skies. Scout both sites beforehand, study where the sun will stand above the ruins, and decide which offers the strongest alignment — and the easiest access — on eclipse morning.
6. Djémila, Algeria
Location: Djémila, Algeria
Start of totality and duration: 10:02 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 2 seconds
Historical cloud cover: 11%
Altitude of eclipsed sun: 50 degrees above east-southeast
Djémila trades a long eclipse for one of the most spectacular settings on the path of totality. Known to the Romans as Cuicul, this exceptionally well-preserved city was built in mountainous terrain around 2,950 feet (900 meters) above sea level — an unusual setting for a Roman settlement — and its ruins include temples, forums, houses, baths, arches and a theater. The surrounding green hills and mountains give eclipse photographers a very different backdrop from the flatter, more arid landscapes farther south. The catch is totality, which is significantly shorter than at other Roman ruins.
7. Sbeitla, Tunisia
Location: Kasserine, Tunisia
Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 19 seconds
Historical cloud cover: 4%
Altitude of sun: 54 degrees above east-southeast
Sbeitla could be one of the great archaeological settings for the 2027 eclipse. Known in Roman times as Sufetula, the city prospered under Roman rule and today contains some of Tunisia's most impressive ancient ruins. Its centerpiece is an unusual group of three remarkably well-preserved temples dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, standing above the forum and reached through the monumental Arch of Antoninus Pius. That high sun will require some careful positioning and probably a wide-angle composition, but eclipse photographers will have an extraordinary collection of arches, columns and temples to use as foregrounds.
8. El Jem Amphitheater, Tunisia
Location: El Djem, Tunisia
Start of totality and duration: 10:09 a.m. CET; 4 minutes, 23 seconds
Historical cloud cover: 2%
Altitude of eclipsed sun: 56 degrees above east-southeast
It may be the third-largest and one of the best-preserved Roman amphitheaters in the world, but El Jem offers another reason to consider it for totality. Unlike Rome's Colosseum — which it closely resembles — visitors can explore its multi-tiered seating, climb high into the surviving structure for panoramic views and visit the underground passages once used by gladiators and animals. Built around A.D. 238, El Jem combines one of Rome's greatest surviving monuments with some of the most promising eclipse conditions on the entire track.
Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

articles.title: A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes
articles.text:
A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes
- Date:
- November 8, 2026
- Source:
- Pennington Biomedical Research Center
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that a buildup of a protein called Miro1 may be a hidden driver of insulin resistance in Type 2 diabetes, with preclinical experiments showing that removing it restores the muscles’ response to insulin. Exercise was also found to lower Miro1 levels in people with diabetes, revealing a potential new pathway for treating the disease.
- Share:
Researchers have identified a protein that may play an important role in Type 2 diabetes by interfering with the body's ability to respond to insulin. The discovery could provide a promising new target for treatments designed to improve blood sugar control.
The protein, known as Miro1, was found at higher levels in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes. In preclinical experiments, scientists discovered that removing Miro1 restored the muscles' response to insulin. They also found that exercise lowered Miro1 levels in people with the disease, offering new insight into how physical activity improves insulin sensitivity.
The findings were published in Nature Communications and could help researchers better understand the biological processes behind insulin resistance, a central feature of Type 2 diabetes.
How a Hidden Muscle Protein Affects Insulin Resistance
Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase1) is located on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells responsible for producing energy. Researchers believe that excessive amounts of this protein may interfere with how muscles respond to insulin, making it more difficult for the body to regulate blood sugar effectively.
To investigate this connection, the research team studied Miro1 in laboratory cells, preclinical models, and people living with Type 2 diabetes. By examining the protein across these different settings, they were able to explore its effects on muscle function and determine whether the findings could be relevant to human disease.
The results showed that Miro1 buildup impaired the muscles' response to insulin. When researchers removed the protein in preclinical models, insulin responsiveness returned, providing evidence that Miro1 contributes directly to this process.
Exercise Reduces a Protein Linked to Type 2 Diabetes
The researchers also investigated whether exercise could influence Miro1 levels in people with diabetes. In a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and Type 2 diabetes, they compared the effects of aerobic exercise with those of standard medical care.
People assigned to the exercise group experienced a decline in Miro1 levels in their muscles. These changes occurred alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity and the muscles' capacity to produce energy.
The findings suggest that reducing Miro1 may be one of the ways exercise helps the body respond more effectively to insulin. They also raise the possibility that treatments designed to target the protein could eventually provide additional benefits alongside physical activity.
"Insulin resistance in muscle is at the heart of Type 2 diabetes, and its molecular causes have remained frustratingly unclear. This study, the product of years of work, identifies Miro1 as a key part of the answer. By tracing Miro1 from cells to preclinical models to patients, we show that Miro1 accumulation impairs the muscle's response to insulin, that removing it causally restores that response in our models, and that exercise reverses its buildup in people. For the field, this is a new therapeutic target. For patients, it deepens our understanding of why exercise is so effective and opens a path toward treatments that could one day complement it," said Dr. John P. Kirwan, the study's senior author.
A Promising New Direction for Diabetes Treatment
Kirwan recently became executive director of the OU Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma. He carried out the research while working at LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and has since brought his internationally recognized translational research program to the University of Oklahoma.
He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the university and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.
The study's first author, Elizabeth Heintz, is a doctoral candidate who worked in the Integrated Physiology and Molecular Medicine Laboratory at Pennington Biomedical. Christopher Axelrod, the study's co-corresponding author, has also moved to the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, joining Kirwan in continuing this line of research.
Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical, emphasized the importance of connecting laboratory discoveries with research involving patients and broader populations.
"This research exemplifies the breadth of scientific discovery at Pennington Biomedical, where research spans all levels, from basic science that reveals the biological mechanisms underlying disease to clinical studies and population-based research that informs public health," said Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical. "Dr. Kirwan and his team's findings on Miro1 demonstrate the value of this integrated approach, connecting fundamental discoveries about muscle function with insights into insulin resistance and the benefits of exercise in people with Type 2 diabetes. This work is advancing our understanding of diabetes and helping lay the foundation for future approaches to prevention and treatment."
Could Targeting Miro1 Lead to New Diabetes Therapies?
Although the results are encouraging, scientists still need to establish whether directly targeting Miro1 can produce safe and effective treatments for people with Type 2 diabetes. The restoration of insulin responsiveness was demonstrated in preclinical models, while the human trial showed that exercise reduced Miro1 levels alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity.
Kirwan plans to continue investigating these findings at the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. His research will combine laboratory experiments with studies involving people to uncover more of the biological mechanisms responsible for diabetes and explore new strategies for preventing and treating the condition.
"Type 2 diabetes is an affliction in Oklahoma and nationally," he said. "Ultimately, we are looking for cures, and we hope these recent findings could be part of the solution."
The study received funding from the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the National Institute on Aging, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

articles.title: Risk of pregnancy loss tied to common antibiotic for acne and infections
articles.text:
A widely used antibiotic for acne and infections is linked to risk of pregnancy loss, new study finds
A common antibiotic may be linked to a higher risk of miscarriage and stillbirth when used early in pregnancy, a new study suggests.
Taking doxycycline, a commonly prescribed antibiotic, during the first trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of pregnancy loss, a new study suggests.
The antibiotic is broad-spectrum, meaning it targets a wide range of bacteria. It's often used to treat acne, respiratory infections and sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia and syphilis. Doctors generally avoid prescribing the drug during the second and third trimesters because it belongs to a class of antibiotics that can bind to calcium in developing bones. Animal studies suggest that this may disrupt fetal bone development.
However, evidence on doxycycline's safety during early pregnancy has been mixed and limited. The new study, published Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, provides clearer evidence of a link between doxycycline use in the first trimester and pregnancy loss.
"I would advise physicians to carefully consider the benefit-risk balance when prescribing doxycycline to women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy," study first author Almut Winterstein, a pharmacist and drug-safety researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science in an email.
A higher risk than other antibiotics
Using information from two U.S. insurance databases, the researchers analyzed 224,870 pregnancies in people ages 12 to 55. More than 218,230 of these patients were treated for respiratory tract infections, and over 6,630 were treated for acne, between conception and the end of the first trimester. About 4,385 of the women filled a prescription for doxycycline during that time frame, while the others received an alternative antibiotic.
Among women with respiratory infections, those prescribed doxycycline had a 40% to 54% higher risk of pregnancy loss, compared with those prescribed amoxicillin, another broad-spectrum antibiotic in a different class. The exact level of risk varied between the two databases.
The researchers also compared the doxycycline users against women prescribed macrolides, the class of antibiotics that includes azithromycin (or "Z-Pak"). Again, the doxycycline users saw a higher risk — 39% and 36% higher, respectively.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Among the patients treated for acne, doxycycline users had a 49% higher risk of pregnancy loss in one database than those given the antibiotic clindamycin. In the second database, though, the difference wasn't statistically significant. Winterstein said that may be because there were fewer patients included in that analysis.
Overall, doxycycline was associated with seven to 11 additional pregnancy losses per 100 pregnancies, compared with the other antibiotic options assessed, the researchers reported.
What drives the risk?
It is not yet clear how the drug might contribute to pregnancy loss. Because the study was observational, it cannot prove that the antibiotic itself caused those losses, which included miscarriages and stillbirths. (Miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of pregnancy, whereas stillbirth refers to pregnancy loss after the 20th week.)
Animal studies hint that doxycycline could interfere with early placental development, potentially making it harder for the placenta to support a growing pregnancy, Luke Grzeskowiak, an associate professor and clinical pharmacist at Flinders University in Australia who was not involved in the study, said in an email.
The study authors also noted in their report that the drug may have direct effects on the developing embryo. But these explanations remain hypothetical; the researchers have not established that either mechanism occurs in humans.
"Pregnancy loss affects around one in four pregnancies and can happen for many reasons," Grzeskowiak noted. Although doxycycline exposure may add to that risk, taking the antibiotic does not necessarily mean pregnancy loss will occur. The available data suggests that it is just one risk factor among many.
Because doxycycline may be prescribed before a pregnancy is recognized, doctors should consider the possibility of pregnancy when prescribing this drug to women of reproductive age, particularly those who are sexually active, Grzeskowiak suggested. That does not mean doctors should avoid prescribing the antibiotic to these women, he emphasized; rather, clinicians should consider pregnancy plans and medical history when choosing a treatment.
In some cases, doxycycline may still be the best option for a severe infection, Winterstein told Live Science, and that infection could itself put a pregnancy at risk. But for less-serious infections, safer alternatives may be available, she said.
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Doxycycline and risk for pregnancy loss: A multi-database, multi-indication cohort study. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/annals-26-01647
Isha Ishtiaq is a freelance health journalist based in Pakistan who covers health, medicine and biomedical research. Her work has appeared in Live Science, Science News, and Medscape, among other outlets. She holds a B.S. (Hons) in biotechnology from the University of Gujrat and an M.S. in biological sciences from the University of Sialkot, where her research focused on the use of deep learning models for disease detection.

articles.title: Astronomers stunned after James Webb Space Telescope discovers the earliest pair of black hole-powered quasars
articles.text:
Astronomers stunned after James Webb Space Telescope discovers the earliest pair of black hole-powered quasars
"There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our universe, much less two."
Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have discovered the oldest pair of supermassive black hole-powered quasars ever seen. There's just one problem: they shouldn't exist!
The compact quasar pair, spotted with the aid of the Gemini North telescope, has been designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, which means "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the universe." The compact quasar pair is seen as it was 900 million years after the Big Bang at a time when such supermassive black holes should not have had time to grow to such tremendous masses.
Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua isn't just the oldest and most distant quasar pairing ever seen. There is just 18,100 light-years, or roughly one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way, between the supermassive black holes, which have masses of 1.5 billion and 400 million times that of the sun. That makes Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua the most compact quasar pair found during a period of the universe's history known as Cosmic Dawn, shortly after the birth of the first stars, galaxies, and black holes.
"There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our universe, much less two," research team leader Silvia Onorato of the NOIRLab said in a statement.
"We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the universe was only a thirteenth of its age and, astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today."
How were supermassive black holes over fed at Cosmic Dawn
Quasars occur when the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of large galaxies are surrounded by a flattened cloud of swirling gas and dust called an "accretion disk," from which they feed or "accrete" matter. The immense gravity of the central black hole causes friction, heating the accretion disk and causing it to glow, often brighter than the combined light of every star in the surrounding galaxy. We see that glow as a quasar.
Finding such objects in the recent cosmic history of the 13.8-billion-year-old universe isn't troubling, though finding compact pairs of them is still extremely rare. Such pairs should be common because the merger of galaxies that brings together supermassive black holes is frequent. That should lead to an abundance of pairs of quasars with a separation less than the typical size of a galaxy. 
There are three reasons this has proven tricky. Firstly, the "quasar phase" of a supermassive black hole is relatively short on cosmic terms. Secondly, even relatively close quasar pairs are very far away, making them faint and hard to detect with ground-based telescopes. Finally, at such great distances and with such a small separation between the two supermassive black holes, the individual members of a quasar pair are hard to individually resolve.
Yet, astronomers do find quasar pairs. Sometimes at distances and times that they would probably rather not, because it challenges everything we know about black hole growth.
The trouble arises before the universe was 1 billion years. That is because, according to current models, black holes should need at least 1 billion years to feed and merge enough to reach masses millions or billions of times that of the sun.
Yet, since it began operations in 2022, the JWST has been routinely discovering supermassive black holes powering quasars as early as 400 million years after the Big Bang. If that wasn't confusing enough, the discovery of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the third quasar pair seen at Cosmic Dawn, could really break current models.
Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua was uncovered in data from the JWST's Aether survey, which is conducting a census of objects in the early universe. Using JWST’s NIRSpec (Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit) instrument, the survey has uncovered 200 quasars, just under half of all currently known early universe quasars. It was while browsing the Aether dataset that the team discovered that quasar J1602+4228A is not alone, it had a companion now designated J1602+4228B.
Resolving these two quasars should have been nearly impossible from the ground. But this was possible for Gemini North thanks to perfect timing and perfect weather conditions over Maunakea, the dormant volcano on the island of Hawai'i where the telescope is located.
A definite scientific feat, Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua remains a mystery for now, but it could actually help scientists better understand how galaxies were coming together during Cosmic Dawn, a vital stage in the evolution of the universe.
"Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," Onorato said. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times."
The team's results were published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

articles.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
articles.text:
Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
- Date:
- November 8, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - San Diego
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.
- Share:
Far below the ocean's surface, a constant snowfall drifts through the darkness. But unlike the frozen flakes that fall from the sky, this underwater snow consists of tiny clumps of waste, dead organisms, and other debris. Known as marine snow, these particles contain everything from mucus and animal feces to silt and the remains of microscopic plankton.
As this material sinks, it carries enormous quantities of carbon from the upper ocean toward the seafloor. Researchers estimate that marine snow removes more than 10 gigatons of carbon from surface waters each year. Yet only about two gigatons reach depths where that carbon can remain stored for hundreds or even thousands of years.
Why so much carbon fails to make it into the deep ocean has long puzzled scientists. Now, researchers from UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln have identified a surprisingly important factor: how sticky the marine snow is.
Their findings, published October 8 in the journal Science, show that the viscosity, or thickness and gooeyness, of marine snow influences how quickly bacteria break it apart and how far it can sink. According to the researchers, the stickiest particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as particles with a thinner, less viscous consistency.
How Ocean Slime Helps Store Carbon
Marine snow plays an important role in Earth's carbon cycle, the natural movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living organisms. By transporting carbon into deep water, sinking particles can keep some of it isolated from the atmosphere for centuries or longer.
However, not every particle survives the journey. Bacteria feed on marine snow as it descends, gradually breaking down the material and affecting how much carbon reaches the ocean's depths.
The new research provides the first detailed look at how living bacteria interact with the physical structure of marine snow and, more broadly, mucus itself. These interactions are important well beyond the ocean's carbon cycle. Similar relationships between bacteria and mucus help sustain coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive systems of humans and other animals.
Until recently, scientists lacked the technology to observe these interactions at the microscopic scale needed to understand them.
A Four-Year Quest to See Inside Marine Snow
The project began in 2021, when Bryce Inman, then a postdoctoral researcher at Scripps Oceanography, set out to explore what he calls "the muscoscape."
"Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible," said Inman.
Together with colleagues including Farooq Azam, a microbiologist and professor emeritus at Scripps, Inman spent four years trying to overcome that limitation. Multiple attempts were unsuccessful before the team finally developed a working technique in 2025.
Their solution combined 3D confocal microscopy with specially designed fluorescent molecules. Confocal microscopy uses light to capture detailed images at different depths within a sample, allowing researchers to reconstruct its structure in three dimensions. The fluorescent molecules helped make features of the material visible.
For the first time, the scientists could examine the "physical terrain" of individual marine snow particles while watching how living bacteria moved through and interacted with them.
The images revealed a surprisingly intricate microscopic environment, complete with structural differences that affect where bacteria can settle and how easily they can reach the material inside.
Why Stickier Marine Snow Sinks Deeper
Much like snowflakes in the atmosphere, marine snow particles vary considerably. Each contains its own mixture of organic and inorganic materials, creating differences in composition, structure, and viscosity.
The researchers' new imaging approach, described in a companion study published in Nature Communications, revealed that bacteria preferentially colonize areas near a particle's surface where the material is less viscous.
The denser, stickier regions deeper inside are much harder for bacteria to penetrate.
"Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down," said Inman. "Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through"
This difference has important consequences for how long marine snow remains intact.
In laboratory experiments, the scientists observed that particles with greater viscosity resisted bacterial degradation and fragmentation for longer periods. Computer simulations further suggested that these stickier particles can descend to greater depths before breaking apart.
Based on these results, the team estimates that highly viscous marine snow can deliver more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.
The findings help explain why some sinking material transports carbon much farther into the ocean than other particles, even though both begin their journeys near the surface.
"How far marine snow can sink is a surprisingly complicated problem, and we have added another - very gooey - piece to the puzzle," said Inman.
A Discovery With Implications Beyond the Ocean
Although the research focuses on marine snow, its implications extend to many environments where bacteria interact with mucus.
Mucus is often regarded as a relatively simple, slippery substance. But the new imaging technology reveals that it has a complex internal landscape, with microscopic structures that can influence how bacteria behave.
Understanding these physical features could help scientists investigate biological processes in settings ranging from human digestive health to the recovery of damaged coral reefs.
The method also opens opportunities to explore interactions that previously could not be observed directly, providing researchers with a new way to study the microscopic environments inhabited by bacteria.
Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, "has a surprising amount of structure," Inman said. "There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we're really examining this physical habitat."
The discovery adds an important missing piece to scientists' understanding of how carbon travels through the ocean. It also demonstrates that something as seemingly ordinary as the thickness of underwater slime can have far-reaching consequences for the planet's natural systems.
Additional funding for the research was provided by the Simons Foundation and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - San Diego. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- Bryce G. Inman, Stuart Humphries, Farooq Azam. Marine snow viscosity regulates microbial degradation and the ocean carbon sink. Science, 2026; 394 (6820): 202 DOI: 10.1126/science.adx4170
- Bryce G. Inman, Nirav Patel, Gabriel Castro-Falcón, Taylor Hernandez, Ryan J. McGorty, Aki H. Ohdera, Logan M. Gonzalez, Kay D. Bidle, Farooq Azam, Stuart Humphries. Molecular rotors reveal the 3D viscous habitat of mucus-colonizing bacteria. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75892-y

articles.title: 125,000-year-old stone points discovered in Saudi Arabia may be world’s oldest poisoned weapons
articles.text:
125,000-year-old poisoned stone points discovered on shore of ancient lake in Saudi Arabia
Archaeologists have discovered thousands of stone artifacts in Saudi Arabia, some of which suggest people were using poison-tipped stone tools to hunt large game 125,000 years ago.
Archaeologists have found what may be the world's oldest poisoned weapons at a 125,000-year-old site on an ancient lakeshore in Saudi Arabia. The stone tools, which were likely used to hunt large animals, had traces of residue from a poisonous tree historically used for its toxins.
"At 125,000 years old, these would be substantially older than the poisoned arrowheads recently identified in South Africa, which date to around 60,000 years ago," study co-author Chris Clarkson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany and Griffith University in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "But we haven't demonstrated exactly how the poison was prepared or whether it was effective. So I'd describe these as potentially the oldest evidence for poisoned hunting weapons, rather than an unequivocally established first."
In the new study, published Thursday (Nov. 12) in the journal Science, researchers investigated a 125,000-year-old site in southern Saudi Arabia known as 'Uruq Aljelibah, which means "sand dunes of a watering hole," study co-author Frans van Buchem, a geologist at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia, told Live Science.
Today, the area is "hot, extremely dry, with extensive sand dunes," Clarkson said, located as it is within the Empty Quarter — one of the hottest, driest deserts on Earth. But the scientists found the site was once home to a freshwater lake measuring about 130 square miles (340 square kilometers) and up to 95 feet (29 meters) deep. Fossils there suggest it once supported a rich diversity of flora and fauna, including hippopotamuses, buffalo, ostriches, camels, gazelles, oryx, palms, reeds, trees and shrubs, which early modern humans likely exploited for food and other resources.
"The idea of hippopotamuses and enormous buffalo living around a lake in what is now the Empty Quarter really brings home just how dramatically these landscapes, and global climates, have changed," Clarkson said.
Astonishing stone tools
The archaeologists discovered more than 5,500 stone artifacts at the site, along with extraordinarily preserved traces of plant materials, such as fibers, resins and wood. Several of these artifacts were stone points that showed impact damage consistent with hunting large animals, and a microscopic analysis revealed traces of animal tissue near the point tips. The distribution of the stone tools closely matched clusters of animal bones, suggesting that the lakeshore was a focal point for hunting and processing game, according to the study.
"At most Paleolithic sites, we're lucky if we get the stone tools and perhaps a few animal bones," Clarkson said. "Here we can actually begin to reconstruct what those tools were doing and what other materials people were combining with them."
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The researchers found that people may have hunted animals with poison-tipped tools. Several stone points had chemical residues linked with the arrow poison tree (Acokanthera schimperi), which is known historically for its toxins and is native to eastern and central Africa and southern Arabia. African hunters have coated spear tips and arrowheads with extracts from this plant to paralyze or kill game.
It remains unclear how hunters who poisoned their targets might have avoided poisoning themselves upon eating the game.
"The effects of a poison depend on the substance, the dose and how it enters the body," Clarkson said. "A poison introduced directly into a wound doesn't necessarily behave in the same way when swallowed." Hunters throughout history "are known to sometimes remove the meat around the wound before eating the rest of the animal," he added.
These findings emphasize how researchers have often underestimated the technological complexity of early human populations, because so much of what they made was organic and has simply disappeared," Clarkson said. "These weren't just people knocking stone flakes off cores," Clarkson noted. "They were combining stone with wood, plant fibers, resins and potentially toxic substances to make complex tools and weapons."
To have so much evidence for how people were making and using tools in a site like this "is remarkable," Eleanor Scerri, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany who did not take part in this research, told Live Science in an email. "This goes from both the micro-scale, in finding traces of how people hafted spear tips, for instance, up to the bigger scale of the whole site and the very convincing spatial relationship between hunting-related tools and the bones of animals such as hippos."
Sites in Arabia that possess both stone tools and animal bones are rare, Jeffrey Rose, a Paleolithic archaeologist at the University of Algarve in Portugal who did not participate in this study, told Live Science in an email. "This one has thousands of artifacts on an old lakeshore alongside hippo, buffalo and ostrich, and some of the flakes fit back together, so the tools were made on the spot," he said. "It's valuable new data."
Out of Africa
The Arabian Peninsula sits between Africa and the rest of Asia and was a major corridor for humans as they dispersed across the world. Recurring spans of increased rainfall could have made its otherwise hostile landscapes more habitable in the past. However, the hot desert that now covers much of Arabia has made it difficult for scientists to excavate many details about this vital bridge during this critical point in human history.
The researchers did not unearth any human remains. Still, they suspect the site most likely belonged to modern humans (our species, Homo sapiens), as opposed to a different human species.
"We know that H. sapiens had already expanded out of Africa and were present in Southwest Asia during this period," Clarkson said. "The age of the site fits with those early movements."
These findings add to growing evidence that wetter intervals in Arabia created migration corridors between Africa and Asia and supported productive habitats capable of sustaining repeated human occupation.
"What our site shows is that people weren't necessarily just passing through these environments," Clarkson said. "They were exploiting them in quite sophisticated ways, using a range of technologies and resources."
But Rose cautioned that all of the stone artifacts found in this study were collected from the surface. "Not one was excavated from the layers that were dated," he said. "The 125,000-year date belongs to the lake, not to the tools. For the tools, it is only a maximum age." Future research at the site should look for stone artifacts sealed in lake beds. "That's hard in Arabia, where wind has stripped most sites down to surface scatters, but it can be done," Rose said.
- Neanderthals may have trekked through the Saudi Arabian desert 55,000 years ago, farther south than experts thought possible
- 1,200-year-old gold hoard discovered in Saudi Arabia may have been buried by a medieval pilgrim
- Life-size rock art points the way to oldest human inhabitants of Saudi Arabia — and the desert oases they used
Clarkson agrees that further work is needed. "I'd really like to keep going back to this site to find more fossils, both animals as well as hopefully human fossils," Clarkson said. "I'd also really like to push the chemical and functional analyses further, particularly the evidence for toxic plant compounds. It would be fascinating to determine exactly which substances were being used, how they might have been prepared and whether they were deliberately applied to hunting weapons."
Future research focusing on the ancient lake margins may reveal more information. "There must be other places where people were living and carrying out activities, and some may preserve better stratified archaeological deposits," Clarkson said.
But the combination of discoveries at this site is amazing, the researchers said.
"I've spent much of my career studying stone tools, and one of the great frustrations is that we're usually only looking at the small fraction of ancient technology that survives," Clarkson said. "Here we have a chance to see much more of the complete technological system."

articles.title: SpaceX launches 2nd mystery mission for US Space Force in 6-day span (video, photos)
articles.text:
SpaceX launches 2nd mystery mission for US Space Force in 6-day span (video, photos)
SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span.
A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627.
Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast.
We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified. Some experts have speculated, however, that each mission launched a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military branch track potential targets around the world.
SpaceX didn't reveal details about either USSF-627 or USSF-432, and the company ended the webcast of both launches shortly after the first stages of their Falcon 9 rockets came back to Earth.
In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean.
It was the seventh mission for USSF-627's Falcon 9 booster, which carries the designation 1103.
NROL-179 | SDA-T1TL-E | SDA-T1TL-A | 3 Starlink missions
USSF-627 was the 120th Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the rocket's 15th national-security flight of the year to date. Eighty-five of the 120 flights have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink broadband constellation in low Earth orbit, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.
The Falcon 9 is not on a record-breaking cadence this year. In 2025, the rocket flew a whopping 165 missions, and 122 of them were Starlink flights.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.
