articles.title: Here are the 25 original Xbox games you can now play on PC
articles.text:
For the 25th anniversary of Xbox, Microsoft is beginning to make good on its paid “next-gen game preservation” promise. Starting today, you can play 25 different original Xbox games on your Windows PC, as long as you have (or are willing to pay) for digital copies.
Here are the 25 original Xbox games you can now play on PC
Microsoft’s adding achievements to original Xbox games for the first time, too.
In July, Microsoft originally launched the idea with just four Xbox games, so 25 is progress, and Microsoft says all these games are now playable with keyboard and mouse.
Plus, Microsoft says it’s adding achievements to original Xbox games for the first time, starting with four games: Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and its sequel, Blinx: The Time Sweeper, and Conker: Live and Reloaded. You can unlock achievements playing them on Xbox One and Xbox Series consoles as well, after a system update. More games should get them in future.
Here’s the full list of Xbox on PC games, with the 21 new additions in bold:
- Armed and Dangerous
- Blinx: The Time Sweeper
- Conker: Live and Reloaded
- Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge
- Disney’s Chicken Little
- The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind
- Fuzion Frenzy
- Grabbed by the Ghoulies
- Indiana Jones and the Emperor’s Tomb
- Red Faction II
- Secret Weapons Over Normandy
- Star Wars Battlefront
- Star Wars Battlefront II
- Star Wars Episode III: Revenge of the Sith
- Star Wars Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy
- Star Wars Jedi Knight II Jedi Outcast
- Star Wars: Jedi Starfighter
- Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic
- Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II – The Sith Lords
- Star Wars: Republic Commando
- Star Wars: Starfighter – Special Edition
- Star Wars: The Clone Wars
- Thrillville
- TimeSplitters 2
- TimeSplitters: Future Perfect
Yes, that’s a lot of Star Wars games, most of which already have a PC version, and few games that were exclusive to Xbox at the time. (But many of those Star Wars games were excellent.)
You also won’t be able to use an original Xbox disc to play these games, I’m afraid, as original Xbox (and Xbox 360) discs aren’t part of Microsoft’s disc-to-digital program; they predate the unique serial number that Microsoft embedded into Xbox One discs. In case you’re wondering, Xbox on PC backward compatibility appears to be powered by an emulator.
Also, most of the new games aren’t currently included with Xbox Game Pass, according to Microsoft; just Blinx, Conker, Crimson Skies, Fusion Frenzy, Morrowind, and Grabbed by the Ghoulies.
Leaked Microsoft documents previously showed us that October 2026 would be the “full launch” of original Xbox games on PC, while Xbox 360 games would have a “gradual” rollout to next-gen consoles between 2027 and 2028, which are when Microsoft is expected to roll out a handheld and a Helix box respectively. The way things are shaping up, the Xbox Helix should play games from every generation of Xbox, even if Helix fundamentally turns out to be a Windows PC.

articles.title: Cyberattack on Fireworks AI allowed hackers to access Notion customers' chat transcripts | TechCrunch
articles.text:
A cyberattack at Fireworks AI has exposed some of its customers’ data, the company has confirmed. Fireworks AI, a platform that developers use to access and use open AI models, said an attacker breached its cloud provider to gain access to a Fireworks development system, which allowed access to some of its customers’ data.
The company said in its latest security advisory that the cybercriminals took Fireworks’ customers’ billing information and some datasets. Fireworks touts tens of thousands of customers worldwide using its platform, including legal tech company Harvey and AI company Cursor.
At least one confirmed affected customer is online document editor and notetaker Notion, which said in a disclosure that the breach affected around 1% of its own customers.
Notion said that Fireworks alerted the company to a security incident and later confirmed that the hackers had stolen some Notion customer data. On November 3, Notion said it disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleted the data stored in its systems, and stopped all connectivity between the two.
Notion confirmed this week that the hackers took chat transcripts of its Notion AI customers who used the “Insights” feature. The company said that the transcripts include “any input to or output from the model that was written to the chat,” but added that much of the data was unattributable and could not be determined from which customer it was obtained.
The breach at Fireworks AI shows how tech companies are reliant on other tech providers for their own offerings, and how cyberattacks can, as a result, spill over into other customers.
Fireworks said that it believes the hackers are financially motivated and that their goals are focused on selling tokens from breaching access to large language models, or LLMs. These schemes rely on selling to unauthorized third parties, who can burn through AI model usage without using their own resources.
This is the second breach affecting Fireworks in as many months, following a security incident in October.

articles.title: CCTV Script 13/11/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on November 13, 2026.
SpaceX's announcement of plans to invest in building data centers in Arizona and Texas coincides with Democratic midterm election victories in both states. Consequently, SpaceX's decision to push ahead against political headwinds has sparked market skepticism regarding whether these projects can materialize smoothly.
In fact, given the current policy and permitting environments in both states, SpaceX's decision is not entirely without basis. Arizona's incumbent governor does not support a blanket moratorium on data center projects, having suspended only related tax credits, which limits the practical impact on project execution. Meanwhile, industry rumors in Texas suggest that the existing data center moratorium could be lifted soon. If true, developers would gain a brief permitting window before the new governor takes office in January, allowing them to submit concentrated applications for air quality, construction, and onsite power generation permits.
Some observers argue that the impact of midterm election outcomes on data center construction need not be overstated. First, community opposition to data centers predated the midterm elections rather than being purely a post election reaction, and many communities remain supportive. Second, against a backdrop of robust long term demand for artificial intelligence compute capacity, data center expansion will persist, though its pace is expected to moderate toward a more rational trajectory.
CHRIS GRISANTI 
Chief Market Strategist 
MAI Capital Management
"Absolutely. And even the ones that aren't yet on the books are going to get built. The data center math is such that they can afford to do that. They can afford to give out electricity. They can afford to solve water problems and job problems. So the solution is coming."
Furthermore, a report from US investment research firm Bernstein indicates that markets may have overestimated the influence of political factors, noting that roughly two thirds of planned US data center capacity was unlikely to be realized anyway due to practical constraints such as development delays, weak tenant credit profiles, and insufficient developer qualifications.
Given that data center construction intensifies supply pressures on public resources like electricity and water, SpaceX's project in Arizona has already encountered local resident pushback, with roughly 2,400 people signing a petition urging authorities to reject permit applications. Analysts point out that while politicians portray data centers as public enemies driving up utility bills, electricity price hikes occur primarily in regions experiencing power tightness caused by inadequate forward looking grid planning. Conversely, in areas with well planned grids, data centers help spread fixed transmission infrastructure costs, potentially lowering overall electricity rates.
KRISTA TANNER 
President and CEO 
ITC Holdings
"Customers don't pay for transmission as much as they do the absence of transmission. Data centers are having a downward pressure on our rates, and in our Midwest footprint, based in Iowa, our rates are going down 13% next year because of the large load."

articles.title: How the Jensen Huang affair changes the outlook for U.S.-China relations
articles.text:
BEIJING — Prolonged U.S. Congressional scrutiny of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy raises the stakes for already tense relations between the world's two largest economies.
Nvidia's Huang resigned Thursday, and agreed to testify before Congress sometime before Thanksgiving on Nov. 26. House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., told reporters there could be "public hearings for other people or other things down road."
"I worry this incident will deteriorate the atmosphere dramatically in Washington against China, and also export control matters, and also the Trump administration in its way of dealing with China," said a Beijing-based foreign policy researcher, who requested anonymity as academics risk discipline or even removal for speaking to the media.
The researcher warned of a possible return to a situation like that in the 1990s, when a "Chinese-American" nuclear physicist was suspected of sharing nuclear secrets with the Chinese government, resulting in a federal prosecution. The court ultimately dismissed all but one of 59 counts.
Now the bilateral relationship, supported by a fragile trade truce, faces another espionage allegation. And this time it's around the tech executive at the heart of the U.S.-China competition over artificial intelligence.
"This isn't really about Jensen," said Mitch Presnick, non-resident honorary fellow on the Chinese economy, Center for China Analysis at the Asia Society.
He noted how some in Washington prefer measures to exclude China and disagreed with the semiconductor executive's message that American technology needed to be used in China in order to remain relevant to global tech development.
Washington started to restrict Nvidia's ability to sell advanced chips to China in 2022. But the Trump administration eased many Biden-era restrictions in 2025.
Meanwhile, Nvidia's Huang advocated his views across a spectrum of markets from the U.S. to China to Taiwan to Germany.
At the peak of his influence, he shared a banquet table in September with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit in Washington, D.C. The two presidents are next expected to meet alongside the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting from Nov. 18 to 19 in Shenzhen, China.
The political landscape has swiftly changed, with Democrats sweeping U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 and turmoil over subsequent reports about Huang's alleged Beijing spy connection. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair over the weekend.
It remains unclear whether any sensitive information was shared.
China's Foreign Ministry has called the "Chinese spy" allegation unfounded "smears against China."
"The U.S. should stop fabricating the "Chinese spy" narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions," spokeswoman Mao Ning said Thursday, according to an official English translation.
More controls, more unease
But the immediate outcome, analysts predict, is more of the U.S. restrictions that China doesn't want.
"The Nvidia scandal has destroyed the credibility of the biggest corporate lobbyist against U.S. export controls on China," said Arthur Kroeber, partner, Gavekal Dragonomics. "There is now a good chance that Congress will tighten up those rules before the end of this year."
Looking ahead, Kroeber warned Beijing could cut off supplies of rare earths or chipmaking materials if the U.S. tried to restrict China further with the MATCH Act or Affiliates Rule. The measures could, respectively, limit Beijing's access to key tech suppliers in the Netherlands and Japan, and drastically expand export controls to include many subsidiaries.
"So when Trump and Xi meet next week in Shenzhen they will probably agree to keep the uneasy U.S.-China truce going," Kroeber said. "It will just keep getting more and more uneasy."
'Spy balloon' redux
Pressuring China has been a rare area of bipartisan agreement in Washington. Beijing has meanwhile ramped up homegrown alternatives to U.S. tech since Washington restricted Nvidia's ability to sell advanced chips to China in 2022. And even Trump's approval of some Nvidia sales had yet to translate into meaningful orders from China.
"We are going to see the two countries start to decouple again in terms of technology," George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice, The Asia Group, said Thursday, noting "China will double-down on self-reliance."
"I begin to feel the Jensen Huang case feels like more like another 'spy balloon' case," he said.
In early 2023, during the Biden administration, the U.S. shot down what it described as a Chinese surveillance balloon. Beijing called it a weather balloon that had blown off course. But the incident delayed then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken's trip to China by more than four months, following limited engagement amid Covid-19 travel restrictions.
Fast-forward to the Huang affair, and "the timing is no accident here," Presnick said. "We're talking about a very curious set of coincidences, and also the fact that the information came through unnamed sources, and there were other things that were strange about it."
Days after the U.S. midterms, The Financial Times and The New York Times reported, citing sources, that U.S. government intelligence believe China's Ministry of State Security recruited businesswoman Alice Huang to gather information on then-CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang.
"Obviously somebody was looking to do this, and they wanted to ... make the discussion about espionage, and not about American competitiveness," Presnick said.
"The U.S. is thinking [in terms of] U.S. and China, but that's not what China is thinking," he said, pointing to Beijing's trade with fast-growing non-Western economies in Africa and Southeast Asia.
—CNBC's Samantha Subin contributed to this report.

articles.title: Jim Cramer has three lingering questions about Anthropic ahead of its historic IPO
articles.text:
As Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering gets set to take center stage on Wall Street, CNBC's Jim Cramer argued Thursday that several questions remain about the artificial intelligence startup's long-term prospects.
The Claude developer plans to price its shares Nov. 18 and begin trading the following day. In its updated IPO paperwork filed Tuesday, the company outlined plans to offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece. At the high end, the offering would raise $64.35 billion and value Anthropic at up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis.
Despite Anthropic's explosive growth and improving profitability, Cramer called out three uncertainties affecting his evaluation of the investment case:
- How will Anthropic's price cuts affect revenue? Anthropic has recently reduced prices for several Claude models, raising concerns that customers are becoming more cost-conscious or turning to cheaper alternatives. Lower prices could encourage greater usage, while additional charges for faster processing could help offset the cuts. Cramer said he was encouraged that revenue growth remained strong in October despite the reductions, but he wants to see whether that momentum continues in the coming months.
- Where will Anthropic's next $100 billion in revenue come from? Much of Anthropic's extraordinary growth has been driven by Claude Code, its AI coding agent, which has gained traction among enterprise customers. But Cramer questioned whether that product alone can sustain the growth needed to cover the company's roughly $900 billion in future computing commitments. Anthropic has introduced Claude Cowork, industry-specific tools and products designed to compete with Microsoft Office. He said cybersecurity, life sciences and robotics could also become major growth opportunities.
- Will Anthropic's focus on AI safety help or hurt growth? Anthropic has built its reputation around a pledge to develop AI responsibly, with CEO Dario Amodei warning about the potential dangers of increasingly powerful models. Cramer questioned whether that commitment could eventually constrain revenue growth if the company slows the release of advanced models. On the other hand, he said its safety-first approach could prove a competitive advantage as businesses become more cautious about adopting autonomous AI systems.
For now, Cramer remains hesitant to recommend buying Anthropic shares when they begin trading, but said he is still evaluating the deal and its potential risks before making a final call. "For now, I'll just tell you that I'm wary of doing so," he said.

articles.title: From Jell-O to Philadelphia cream cheese, Kraft Heinz is putting a new spin on old favorites
articles.text:
Kraft Heinz is giving some of America's most familiar grocery staples an unexpected makeover in a bid to revive long-slumping sales and win back support from Wall Street.
The packaged food giant — known for brands like Heinz, Kraft, Philadelphia Cream Cheese, Lunchables and Oscar Mayer — is reinventing its decades-old brands to appeal to changing consumer tastes, particularly growing demand for protein and convenient foods, CEO Steve Cahillane told CNBC's Jim Cramer on Thursday.
"I think the mistake that was made at Kraft Heinz before I arrived in the last several years is this notion that there's a 'forever brand,' that brands can just live on the history of their past," Cahillane said after Kraft Heinz held an investor day earlier Thursday. "That's not true. But equally, brands that existed for a long time are not necessarily destined for the dustbin of history."
"You have to innovate. You have to bring new news. You have to bring excitement with your brand," he added.
That philosophy is central to Cahillane's turnaround strategy. Since taking the helm at the start of 2026, he has directed an additional $700 million toward the business and hired 400 employees. He also paused plans to split Kraft Heinz into two companies. At Thursday's investor day, Kraft Heinz projected that it would return to top- and bottom-line growth in the second half of 2027. The company's revenue has declined on an annual basis in back-to-back years, with analysts also projecting a 1% drop in 2026, according to FactSet.
"I saw a lot that was fixable," Cahillane said. "If we spent all of this year separating the business ... we would have ended up with two suboptimal businesses."
He argued that the company's resources could be put to better use revitalizing the company's brands.
One of the clearest examples of that strategy is Kraft Mac & Cheese. The nearly century-old brand has returned to growth following the introduction of products including PowerMac, which packs 17 grams of protein and six grams of fiber, and Restaurant Edition, which brings restaurant-inspired flavors to the classic boxed format.
Perhaps an unexpected innovation is Kraft Mac & Cheese Cheesy Ramen, which debuted in Canada in July to overwhelming demand. "We sold out three months' worth of stock in a week," Cahillane said, adding that the company plans to bring the cheesy noodles to U.S. shelves next year.
Jell-O is also joining the protein craze, which has been fueled in part by fitness influencers and the rise of GLP-1 weight-loss medications. Kraft Heinz plans to introduce pudding with 10 grams of protein, giving the nostalgic dessert a nutritional boost. Cahillane said the company's research and development team worked to overcome the taste and texture challenges that often come with adding protein to familiar foods.
"Our R&D team has cracked the code," he said. "The chocolate's my favorite. Chocolate Jell-O pudding with protein, I think, is going to be a real hit."
Philadelphia cream cheese is next in line for a protein-packed makeover, following the introduction of new flavors of the regular spread in September. Cahillane said Kraft Heinz plans to introduce new products under the brand next year. "We've got a big opportunity to drive protein, to steal some share from cottage cheese, and that's going to come through the Philadelphia name," he said.
Kraft Heinz shares have struggled for years, but investors are showing signs of renewed optimism. The stock has gained 7% this quarter, outperforming the broader market, even as its roughly flat performance for the year trails the S&P 500's 11% advance.

articles.title: Cramer says Jensen Huang betrayed Nvidia shareholders. How to pick up the pieces
articles.text:
CNBC's Jim Cramer criticized former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday for putting the chipmaker's future at risk.
"Did he betray you, the shareholders?" Cramer asked. "Yes. End of story."
Huang resigned Thursday morning following reports of an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Hours later, Reuters reported that he had an "intimate relationship" with a second employee. These revelations came days after Huang admitted to an affair with an executive at a Singapore-based cloud computing company whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China. Longtime CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO of Nvidia. Cramer said Huang's departure was necessary to protect Nvidia from further fallout.
Shares ended Thursday down more than 4%, but at its lows of the morning, the stock was off over 14%. The decline in Thursday's session brings Nvidia's losses this year to 12%.
While questions remain about what comes next for the AI chipmaker, Cramer argued that Nvidia's future extends beyond the executive who helped build it into one of the world's most valuable companies. "There won't be a better Nvidia, just a different one [without Huang]," Cramer said, envisioning a company that is better organized and more disciplined about its investments.
Under Huang, Nvidia built an extensive equity investment portfolio that included a $5 billion investment in Intel in 2025 and a $2 billion investment in AI cloud provider CoreWeave earlier this year. The investments, and many others, were part of Huang's strategy to strengthen Nvidia's position across the AI industry.
During the CNBC Investing Club's Morning Meeting livestream Thursday, Cramer recalled urging Kress to reduce the company's stakes in Intel and CoreWeave, only to be told that Huang preferred to maintain them. Cramer suggested that new leadership could take a more disciplined approach to capital allocation, potentially cashing in on some of those investments and returning the proceeds to shareholders through even bigger stock buybacks.
Cramer expressed confidence in Kress, praising her deep understanding of Nvidia's operations and financials. He argued that the longtime finance chief is well positioned to provide stability as the company navigates the investigations surrounding Huang, which stretch from the boardroom to Washington, D.C.
Nvidia didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment on Cramer's remarks. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Going forward, Nvidia's underlying business remains strong, Cramer said, pointing to its substantial cash reserves and expectations for a robust earnings report Tuesday evening. But he cautioned that even strong quarterly results might not be enough to reassure investors during this time of lingering uncertainty.
Investigations into Huang's conduct and possible violations of U.S. chip export restrictions could result in sanctions that hurt Nvidia's international business. Meanwhile, competitors, including Advanced Micro Devices, are making progress with their own AI chips, potentially threatening Nvidia's market dominance. AMD shares surged almost 6% on Thursday, extending their winning streak to five straight sessions.
Those risks have prompted Cramer to take a more cautious approach to Nvidia stock, particularly after the substantial gains shares have delivered over the years for Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio of 32 stocks managed by the Club. On Tuesday, as Huang's future at Nvidia looked more and more in doubt, the Club downgraded Nvidia to a hold-equivalent rating.
"Don't ever turn a successful investment into an unsuccessful trade," he said, urging longtime shareholders sitting on big gains to consider taking some profits. "You don't want to give up all of your gains if the stock falls further. It fell further today after many of the analysts jumped ship and downgraded the stock from buy to hold. There could be more ahead."
At the same time, Cramer cautioned against giving up on Nvidia altogether, pointing to the company's extensive engineering expertise and multiyear product roadmap as reasons to believe it can continue competing at the forefront of AI without Huang.
The "Mad Money" host also drew parallels to Apple's leadership transition from Steve Jobs to Tim Cook, suggesting that Nvidia could benefit from a similarly capable successor who brings a different management style without sacrificing the company's technological edge.

articles.title: Stock futures rise after market dips amid Nvidia woes: Live updates
articles.text:
U.S. equity futures rose Thursday evening after major indexes dipped and Nvidia shares fell, following the exit of its founder and CEO Jensen Huang amid an ongoing scandal.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 166 points, or 0.3%. S&P 500 futures gained 0.4%, while Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.6%.
The action comes after the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 dropped about 0.4% each in regular trading. The Dow slid almost 190 points, or 0.4%. Nvidia's 4.3% decline dragged down the three major averages, even as the chip stock ended the session off its lows.
Asia-Pacific markets were mixed Friday, with South Korea's Kospi leading gains in the region, up 1.98%. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 1.74% while Australia's S&P/ASX 200 dropped 0.62%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was down 0.58%, and mainland China's CSI 300 on mainland China was 0.22% lower.
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from his post at the chip company following reported extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Analysts told CNBC that Huang's exit could trigger a 20% correction in the stock.
Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress, who's worked at the company for more than a decade, will lead the chipmaker as interim CEO. The company's board is looking both internally and externally for a full-time replacement for Huang.
A jump in oil prices also kept stocks under pressure Thursday, with Brent crude rising more than 3% on the day to settle at $95.82 a barrel. Oil climbed after President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post, "We don't need a deal with Iran." The comment raised concerns that the U.S.-Iran war could drag on further.
Another market catalyst awaits on Friday in the form of October's producer price index reading, a measure of wholesale inflation. Economists polled by Dow Jones see headline PPI rising 0.4% on the month and 6.6% from 12 months earlier.
Even with the latest bout of market turbulence, the major averages are heading for weekly advances. The Nasdaq is up 3.2%, while the S&P 500 is on pace for a 2.9% advance. The Dow is poised for a nearly 2% jump. All three indexes are heading for their best weekly performances since early August.

articles.title: Nscale updates IPO prospectus that shows widening loss
articles.text:
Nvidia-backed neocloud Nscale on Thursday released updated paperwork for a U.S. initial public offering.
The company had a third-quarter net loss of $1.69 billion on $307.5 million in revenue, which was up 1,344% year over year, according to an updated prospectus for its planned initial public offering. The net loss widened from $1.02 billion in the second quarter, when the company generated $140.6 million in revenue, up 1,252%.
London-based Nscale filed to go public in September, but hasn't updated its prospectus since then. The company did not specify how much it intends to raise in the public offering on the New York Stock Exchange.
Since then the company has faced public setbacks.
Microsoft walked away from an Nscale data center that it had planned to use in England. Darren Hardman, Microsoft's CEO for the U.K and Ireland, told CNBC in October that the decision had to do with Nscale's ability to get access to electricity.
The Financial Times reported that Microsoft decided against renewing a contract with Nscale in Texas. The company said in its IPO filing that it expects Microsoft to be a "significant customer in future periods."
The neocloud market, which focuses on renting access to chips such as Nvidia graphics processing units to clients, has been in tumult, partly because Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, after admitting to being unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia is investigating Huang's relationship with a woman whom intelligence agencies have called a Chinese spy.
In October investors pressured shares of Nscale rival CoreWeave, but the stock advanced almost 25% on Wednesday on strong results. CoreWeave pulled back about 7% on Thursday following the departure of Huang, who has overseen investments in the neocloud.
Shares of another neocloud, Nebius, fell about 17% on Thursday, with the company issuing light full-year guidance.
But Nscale can point to growing business with Anthropic, which itself is aiming to go public. In late September Anthropic exercised its right to contract for additional computing power at an Nscale site in West Virginia.

articles.title: Without Jensen Huang, Nvidia's organizational structure isn't 'built to last,' management expert says
articles.text:
Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as CEO of Nvidia, the chipmaking company he co-founded in 1993, following public revelations of his extramarital affairs. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, will serve as the company's interim CEO.
Huang's visionary leadership style and his central role in driving the company's strategy, combined with the company's unusually flat management structure, will make him especially difficult to replace, experts say.
Huang notably had more direct reports than the typical CEO, with a "direct staff" of approximately 60 employees, he said in a March 2026 interview with podcaster Lex Fridman.
"The more direct reports a CEO has, the less layers are in the company. It allows us to keep information fluid," Huang told CNBC's Andrew Ross Sorkin in 2023.
Having minimal hierarchy has worked for Nvidia so far "because [Huang] has been a strong leader with a strong vision," says Jo-Ellen Pozner, associate professor of management at Santa Clara University's Leavey School of Business.
But that structure could make the company's leadership shake-up even more difficult to navigate, she says.
Functioning without an 'orchestrator'
At companies with flat management structures, the CEO often has even more influence than they would in a traditional hierarchy, according to Joseph Fuller, professor of management practice at Harvard Business School.
Nvidia's structure was "designed to adapt well in a world of change, either caused by us or affecting us," Huang said in a March 2025 conversation with Arthur Mensch, cofounder and CEO of Mistral.
Since he directly managed the company's top executives, Huang held "a tremendous amount of power" at Nvidia, Fuller says. "He's the orchestrator," he continues. "He's the coordinator. He's resolving the disputes. He's allocating the resources."
Now, the company has lost its top decision-maker, Fuller says.
Without Huang, "there is likely nobody who is able to coordinate among those various people with their different expertise and domains," Pozner says, which could lead to a slowdown in technical work.
There are some advantages to Nvidia's flat structure, says Denise Rousseau, professor of organizational behavior and public policy at Carnegie Mellon University. Having fewer management layers can strengthen "local leaders" in each area of the company, she says, which can help stabilize Nvidia through its leadership transition.
But "nobody else has the big picture view" that Huang did, Pozner says, which makes finding a permanent successor within the company especially difficult. Moreover, with dozens of direct reports, it's unlikely that Huang had the time to groom one of his subordinates to take over one day, she says.
Pozner predicts that Nvidia's next leader will steer the company toward a more traditional management structure. "I understand that a lot of people, especially in Silicon Valley, are averse to rigid hierarchies and the kind of structure that we expect from a legacy organization," she says. "But it's functional for a reason."
Ultimately, Nvidia's current system is "not an organizational structure that's built to last," Pozner says.

articles.title: Cisco beats on earnings, says AI infrastructure revenue will double this fiscal year
articles.text:
Cisco shares rose in extended trading on Thursday after the maker of networking gear reported better-than-expected fiscal first-quarter results.
Here's how the company did compared to LSEG consensus estimates:
- EPS: $1.40 adjusted vs. $1.33 expected
- Revenue: $18.5 billion vs. $18.1 billion expected.
Revenue increased 24% from $14.88 billion a year earlier, Cisco said in a statement. Net income rose to $4.6 billion, or $1.14 per share, from $2.9 billion, or 72 center per share, a year ago.
Cisco is trying to gain a foothold in the artificial intelligence buildout after missing out on the early years of the generative AI boom. The company's stock price is up about 35% this year as of Thursday's close, trouncing the Nasdaq, which has gained 9% over that stretch.
Cisco raised its expectation for AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to $9 billion this fiscal year, more than double the figure in fiscal 2026.
"Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era," CEO Chuck Robbins said in the statement.
For the fiscal second quarter, Cisco said it expects revenue of between $18 billion and $18.2 billion, topping the average analyst estimate of $17.88 billion, according to LSEG. The company is projecting adjusted earnings per share of $1.34 to $1.36, beating the $1.23 average estimate.

articles.title: Cerebras surges 17% after beating on quarterly revenue and announcing Microsoft deal
articles.text:
Cerebras Systems reported better-than-expected revenue and quarterly guidance in its earnings report on Thursday, and touted a new deal with Microsoft. The stock soared 17% in extended trading.
Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:
- Loss per share: 67 cents. It's not immediately clear how the number compares with the loss of 14 cents expected
- Core revenue: $230.9 million vs. $214.7 million expected
Cerebras' core revenue grew 70% from $135.7 million, compared with 103% growth in the second quarter, according to a statement.
"I think there is opportunity created by, particularly on the hardware side, the sale of hardware, where long lead times in GPUs and more expense creates opportunity for us," Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman told CNBC in an interview, referring to graphics processing units.
Executives will announce a new relationship with Microsoft, one of the world's top cloud providers, on a conference call with analysts, Feldman said. The call starts at 5 p.m. ET.
"We believe revenue begins to show up in Q1 '27," Feldman said in the interview, adding that Microsoft signed the deal in October. Cerebras has also landed deals with other major cloud providers Amazon and Oracle.
Cerebras is evaluating its financing options to meet the ramping demand, Feldman said in the interview.
The company is trying to challenge Nvidia in the AI chip market. Its earnings land on the same day that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded after multiple scandals involving extramarital affairs.
For the fourth quarter, Cerebras expects a core gross margin of 47% to 49%, with $310 million to $330 million in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for a 42.1% margin and $271 million in revenue.
Cerebras said it expects revenue to triple in 2027. That implies about $2.85 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $2.92 billion.
Cerebras shares have slumped by about 47% since the company debuted on Nasdaq in May.

articles.title: Stocks could be in for a rude awakening if the Fed hikes rates more than expected
articles.text: Stock investors may be underappreciating the pressure the bond market could face, if the prospect of a more aggressive Federal Reserve turns into a serious risk. Bond markets were closed Wednesday for Veterans Day, which gave stocks a reprieve from some of the warning signs in the market on Tuesday. That's when the yield on the 2-year U.S. Treasury — a useful gauge for interest rate expectations — surged 18 basis points to top 4.73%. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield that's used as a benchmark for mortgages and other loans also spiked, rising back above 5%. Yields climbed further when the bond market reopened Thursday, sending the 2-year note to 4.87% and the 10-year above 5.11%. Higher bond yields come after a hotter-than-expected October consumer inflation report cemented the case for a quarter point increase in the fed funds rate at the Fed's December meeting, and raised fears of more hikes in 2027 — a scenario that stock investors have yet to price in. "The Fed is the real risk going out in the intermediate term," Warren Pies, co-founder and strategist at 3Fourteen Research, told " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday. "The market is not priced for another two plus hikes, which are probably coming." Odds of more rate hikes are increasingly creeping into fed funds futures, which were last pricing in three quarter point raises by March, according to the CME FedWatch tool . That would put the target rate in a range between 4.50% and 4.75%, up from 3.75% and 4.00% currently. 'Real indigestion' Stocks are ignoring bonds lately, and with good reason. Last week's AI washout was made worse this week as investors followed news of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affairs, and his subsequent exit from the dominant AI chipmaker early Thursday. Yet the major stock averages held up fairly well Thursday as investors rotated into others corners of the market, with Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom two beneficiaries. But Pies worries the stock market will again turn its attention to inflation at the start of 2027, when price reports could meaningfully worsen as companies make adjustments for the new calendar year — a phenomenon called "residual seasonality" — putting the interest rate outlook front and center for investors. "That's where I think you could start seeing some real indigestion in the equity market," Pies said. Some on Wall Street are already running the numbers on what that could mean. Wolfe Research strategist Chris Senyek said that the typical reaction to the start of a hiking cycle is a 0.6% decline in the stock market over the next three months. Going back to 1972, the median hiking cycle lasts 19 months, with the fed funds rate rising about 3.94 percentage points, although that allows for bouts of rapid inflation and sky-high interest rates in the 1970s and early 1980s. "Our sense is that investors could be mispricing the risk of a longer than expected hiking cycle with the current Fed regime, even if oil prices slowly drift lower," Senyek wrote on Wednesday. At Goldman Sachs, chief U.S. economist David Mericle now expects a third quarter point hike in March, in addition to the quarter point raise he already anticipates in December. He expects softer inflation reports in November and December, and hotter ones in January. December tone But it's also the case that elevated bond yields could coexist with a resilient stock market. Just last month, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury topped 5.3% at the same time as the S & P 500 also climbed to record highs above 7,800. Many expect that a productivity and earnings boom from AI could help companies cope with higher borrowing costs. But generally speaking, higher bond yields hurt stocks. A U.S. 10-year Treasury yield above 5% traditionally knocks the equity market, as investors shift to fixed income securities that give more income at less risk. Higher bond yields also lower the present value of future corporate earnings. For many, the risks to bond yields are tilted up, given ongoing credit demands from the AI buildout, a federal deficit running at 6% or more of gross domestic product and the potential for higher inflation. Steve Englander, head of G10 FX Research at Standard Chartered, is turning his attention to the December Fed meeting, where any tough comments on inflation by Chairman Kevin Warsh could finally cause the stock market to sit up and pay attention, just as the bond market and the U.S. dollar are doing. "If they did a 50 [basis point rate hike], and it's sort of a hawkish 50 by saying, 'Hey, we're doing 50, but we're not done,' that might scare the market," Englander said. Englander's baseline expectation remains just one quarter point hike at the December meeting. But he also expects the 10-year yield could climb to 5.50% by the middle of next year.

articles.title: Widespread Microsoft outage takes down Outlook and other 365 services
articles.text:
Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday that impacted thousands of users across regions, according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.com.
The outage began shortly before 1 p.m. and impacted Microsoft 365 services, Outlook and Teams. At the time, about 130,000 users reported issues with Outlook.
Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site.
"We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online," a Microsoft spokesperson wrote in a statement to CNBC. "We appreciate our customers' patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible."
Microsoft shared updates on the outage from its Microsoft 365 Status account on social media platform X.
Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."
At 4 p.m., Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.
"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."
Microsoft initially said infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions" was responsible for the connectivity problems.
The company later determined that the elevated load was caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure" and that some servers were failing automated health checks.
"We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service," Microsoft wrote.

articles.title: United Airlines won’t let AI agents book your flight. Expert says you shouldn't let a bot do that for you, anyway
articles.text:
United Airlines said Wednesday it would be restricting artificial intelligence bots from its digital platforms, warning that allowing third-party AI assistants to access account credentials could expose sensitive personal information, lead to unintended purchases or other unauthorized account activity. The move is similar to Amazon's recent blocking of Meta's Muse agent from making purchases on its site.
Still, AI agents can complete a wide range of tasks on your behalf. Instead of just asking Muse what the weather will be tomorrow, you can tell it to suggest an outfit based on tomorrow's weather forecast and book you a rideshare if it's going to rain, for example. Or, rather than just creating an itinerary for your next vacation, you can connect a payment option and have your Dot — OpenAI's agent offering — book flights, hotels and excursions for you.
You can even have an AI agent buy and sell stocks through investing platforms like Robinhood.
Relying on an AI agent for any of these tasks may come with mixed results depending on which agent you use, what data you allow it to access and the complexity of the task you've asked it to carry out. Because broadly, agentic AI is still in its infancy, you may not want to let an agent make decisions "anytime [your] health, wealth, or privacy are involved," says Shomit Ghose, adjunct professor at the University of San Francisco School of Management, and lecturer at the University of California, Berkeley College of Engineering.
"You can have agents do interesting things for you, like categorize your spending, or flag unusual charges, or model what-if scenarios," he says. "Those are good things, but bad things would be moving money, making trades, filing forms. All those things should stay manual at this point."
AI-enthusiast traders may need some convincing, though.
Here's what you should consider before outsourcing your whole to-do list to an AI agent.
Context matters
Though AI agents' capabilities are improving, they still operate in a fairly literal sense, which can create problems, Ghose says. If you tell your agent to book you the cheapest flight, for example, it may book you a flight at 3 a.m. or one with three layovers, unless you give the agent specific guardrails.
"The bot only knows your context," Ghose says. "It cannot infer, as we humans are able to do, because of instinct and culture and education."
Further, bots can still get it wrong even with a seemingly clear and direct command. They "treat all data as being equal," Ghose adds. So if it finds information on the web that is either inaccurate or subjective, it could give you misleading guidance or fail to meet your standards for the given task.
For example, if you tell your agent to book you a reservation at a good barbecue restaurant, it may get you a table at a place that claims to be "the best barbecue in the world" on its website. But the restaurant may be in an inconvenient location or have poor reviews elsewhere on the web. Your command may need to be more specific, like asking your agent to check reviews on Google Reviews or Yelp.
'Ask yourself: Does the human need to be in the loop?'
Depending on what task you've assigned the bot, the outcome could be rather innocuous. But when individuals consider letting bots make purchases for them, make changes to their investment portfolios or and the like, the result could be more consequential.
"In the end, you want to ask yourself: Does the human need to be in the loop?" Ghose says.
If you're booking a vacation, for example, it's reasonable to ask an AI agent to help make a decision on your destination based on the weather, your budget and other factors. But actually booking the flights and hotels "should still come back to me," Ghose says. He wants to maintain final say over major financial decisions.
Doing so may even save you money. In Booking Holdings' third-quarter earnings report, the Connecticut-based travel technology company reported 20% higher spending among customers who used AI assistants versus those who didn't to book accommodations on Agoda, one of its travel platforms. It's unclear whether those customers were led to pricier options or did, in fact, seek more expensive amenities. The company doesn't cite a single factor for the finding.
AI agents are also making their way into the healthcare sector, which can pose risks for users too quick to rely on the agents' advice, Ghose says. Letting an AI agent handle prescription refill requests, for example, could be convenient, but AI managing prescriptions more broadly may act on "incomplete records and won't be able to recognize a dangerous interaction or a worsening condition before the action has already taken effect," he says. Generally, a clinician will have to sign off on any new prescriptions, but federal agencies are backing programs that would allow AI agents to assist in diagnostics and prescription management for patients.
Relatedly, anytime you grant an AI agent access to your personal information, whether it's medical records or your email inbox, you could be introducing privacy risks, Ghose says. He recommends users only allow agents to "use limited permission accounts," like letting it access your subscription to a news source, rather than your personal accounts, such as your bank account or credit card information.
For some tasks like investing decisions, you need to have a certain level of expertise to clearly dictate your strategy and goals. And even if you give yourself final say on trades, instead of delegating to the bot, it's essential that you understand the risk involved in moves your AI agent proposes. While a large language model can help you research investments and gather information around an asset, humans are still better at putting that into the context of their individual financial strategy and goals, AI experts say.
Agents can "make your trading experience easier, there is no doubt about it," Shridhar Rathore, an experienced investor who uses agentic trading tools, recently told CNBC Make It. "But [letting agents] make investment decisions, that's where people can lose money if they are not careful...they have to make sure that for the execution, the human is in the loop."
"You want to be really specific and say, 'I am crafting a trading strategy, and these are the kind of things I'm trying to optimize for,'" like whether you're thinking about short or long-term strategy, Ghose says. "So that as [the agent] ingests information, it can treat it with the right context."

articles.title: Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor
articles.text:
Alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, at the same time that she was in business with Nvidia and also reportedly having a romantic affair with its ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei was first discovered by analysts at private intelligence firm Tesari. The firm exclusively shared its findings with CNBC. Tesari, which uses artificial intelligence to collect evidence and specializes in national security investigations around the world, provides intelligence research to private companies and the U.S. government.
This previously unreported entanglement may raise questions about Alice Huang's intent and conduct in her relationship with the CEO and whether Jensen Huang knew his romantic partner was closely connected with his competition. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an affair, though the precise timing of his relationship with Alice Huang is unknown.
The mysterious saga of Alice Huang involves a tangle of interlocking corporations and transactions that show her connection to entities that ultimately provided computing power to Huawei in China.
Huawei is known as a Chinese government "state champion" in the technology and telecommunications sectors, meaning it receives enormous financial support from the government in Beijing so it can lower prices and undercut global competitors. It is considered a key part of the Chinese government's push for global technical dominance and is closely linked to the Chinese Communist Party.
Businesses connected to Alice Huang were linked with supplying Nvidia computing power to Huawei, according to documents reviewed by CNBC, around the same time she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together, in December 2023.
In 2024, Nvidia said Huawei was a top competitor, specifically in artificial intelligence chips including graphics processing units, central processing units and networking chips.
"This activity, which surfaced through our analysis of Alice's network, warrants a national security and [technology] counterproliferation investigation," said Brian Andersen, Tesari's vice president for national security applications and a former supervisory special agent with Homeland Security Investigations.
If the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry Security and Homeland Security Investigations found evidence that anyone transferred "controlled equipment" to Huawei without authorization, potential charges might include export-control violations, conspiracy and smuggling, Andersen said.
The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei is so convoluted that analysts at Tesari told CNBC that based on their previous investigative experience, they suspect it was designed to deliberately obscure the relationship.
Nvidia and Huawei did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. Jensen Huang did not respond to a voicemail left on a mobile phone. Alice Huang could not be reached.
According to Chinese corporate records and media reports compiled by Tesari and provided to CNBC, Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le and who according to documents at the time was based in Hong Kong, in 2019 sold a cloud business she owned called Osmanthus to a Chinese gaming company called 7Road. A subsidiary of 7Road, which was based in Singapore, was spun off as "Megaspeed" in 2023. Megaspeed would go on to become a key Nvidia customer, helping facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, The Information reported Tuesday.
As early as 2016, Alice Huang had also become a co-owner of a financial firm known as Shanghai Hexi, which heavily invests in tech and data centers. In 2021, Hexi in turn acquired 27 percent of a company called Shanghai Century Longteng, a data center developer, which Hexi held until 2024. That firm owned a controlling 50.1 percent stake in a data center facility called Shenzhen Yifeng Technology Co. Ltd. in mainland China.
The key customer of that data center was Huawei Cloud, the Shenzhen, China-based subsidiary of Huawei Technologies.
In addition, Alice Huang's firm Hexi guaranteed the loans required to finance the Shenzhen data center, which did business with Huawei.
Hexi did not immediately respond to a message via its LinkedIn page sent outside of normal business hours.
CNBC translated corporate records and Chinese news articles in Mandarin that Tesari provided.
It's not clear if the Shenzhen data center was able to acquire Nvidia GPUs, but its majority owner began purchasing the chips in 2023. That company is known as Zhejiang Century Huatong Group and is a business partner of Alice Huang's Hexi through their joint ownership of Century Longteng.
That made Alice Huang a part owner of a data center providing computing power to Huawei. And that was happening at around the same time the first known sightings of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang in public together.
And that raises the question of why Huawei, which has access to Chinese-made chips, would need to rent computing power from an outside entity.
Hexi exited its stake in the data center development company in 2024, but individuals within Alice Huang's network are still connected to the Shenzhen data center. Her husband Kang Wei is a longtime business associate who founded Hexi, where Alice Huang previously held an executive role. In 2022, Kang became an executive of Century Longteng, which owns the controlling stake in the Shenzhen data center, and he also attended the company's signing of the Huawei agreement.

articles.title: Who will replace Jensen Huang? Here's our early thoughts on the search for Nvidia's next CEO
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Stocks are showing resilience on Thursday as investors grappled with the fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation amid a widening affair scandal. The S & P 500 is down about 0.25% in afternoon trading. By sector within the S & P 500, energy, communication service, and utilities, consumer staples, and consumer discretionary outperformed. Meanwhile, materials, industrials, and information technology were weaker. Oil is moving back up after President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that the U.S. doesn't need to make a deal with Iran, claiming "we've got their Strait," in reference to the Strait of Hormuz. This suggests the risk of renewed tensions in the Middle East may be higher than the reconciliatory tone expected after the Republicans' midterm losses last week. Bond yields spiked again, continuing the move we saw Tuesday in reaction to a hot consumer price index report . The bond market was closed Wednesday in observance of Veterans Day. Shares of Nvidia are down 5% in afternoon trading, well off their early morning lows of roughly $149 apiece. As uncertainty around Huang's future mounted this week, we downgraded our Nvidia rating Tuesday, and then said Wednesday that we would've been buyers of Advanced Micro Devices if our trading restrictions allowed us. Jim Cramer reiterated our interest in buying AMD during Thursday's Morning Meeting. Huang's resignation may also explain why hyperscalers with their own internal chip programs — namely Alphabet and Amazon — outperformed in Thursday's session. Google parent Alphabet, known for its tensor processing units, is up around 2%. Amazon, which has found great success with its Trainium chips, is up roughly 0.6%. The loss of a visionary founder raises plenty of questions about who will lead Nvidia into the next era. Over our many years of owning Nvidia's stock, listening to every earnings call and following every key corporate event, we've come to view CFO Colette Kress as a rigorous and respected leader who is more than capable of keeping the company on the right path and advancing its AI roadmap. She's a great choice to be the interim chief executive. We'll see what happens with the board's search for a permanent CEO across internal and external candidates. But early chatter suggests this position will be highly sought after from the best and brightest of tech leaders. Ian Buck — Nvidia's vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing and the inventor of its linchpin CUDA software — is a favored candidate. Buck is who Jim suggested take over on Tuesday's "Mad Money," but upon learning more information about Huang's relationships over the past 36 hours, an outside candidate may be more appropriate to clean up the mess. In addition to Wednesday's report in The New York Times about an affair with an executive who reported to him, Reuters on Thursday reported that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee , citing unnamed sources. Trump earlier Thursday suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook as a Huang replacement. We're obviously huge fans of Cook, but we're not sure he would be the best fit to lead the chipmaker. We've also seen the leaders of the cloud units at Alphabet and Amazon mentioned as possible candidates. Additionally, Palo Alto Network CEO Nikesh Arora's name was floated around on "Squawk on the Street" earlier. He's a bankable executive known for dealmaking and his name being out there may explain why Palo Alto shares are down 3% Thursday. The bottom line is that Nvidia lost a key person, and the stock is less attractive than it was a week ago. But the technology roadmap has not changed overnight, and leaders and its employee base will rally around the company and products, which remain best of class. This is why we aren't heading for the exits entirely. But from a portfolio management perspective, on Thursday's Morning Meeting, Jim advised investors sitting on extraordinary gains to pare their positions as part of investment discipline. After the closing bell on Thursday, Cisco Systems and Applied Materials report quarterly results. There are no major earnings reports scheduled for Friday morning. On the economic data side, we'll see the October producer price index report. The hot CPI report Tuesday prompted traders to begin pricing in the possibility of a 50 basis point rate hike at the Federal Reserve's policy meeting next month. Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. If Jim has talked about a stock on CNBC TV, he waits 72 hours after issuing the trade alert before executing the trade. articles.title: Nvidia: Ex-prosecutor Joon Kim and Wachtell, Lipton bring big track record to investigation
articles.text:
Joon Kim, the lawyer tapped by artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia to investigate its former CEO Jensen Huang, and the Big Law firm he works for have a long history of investigating high-profile cases.
Kim, in his career as a top federal prosecutor and as an attorney in private practice, has had in his sights mobster John "The Teflon Don" Gotti's son, former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and other high-profile people and companies.
The law firm that Kim recently joined — Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz — this year conducted an investigation for the NBA of the Los Angeles Clippers and its billionaire owner, Steve Ballmer, which ended with the basketball league imposing stiff sanctions on Ballmer and the Clippers for violating salary cap rules in connection with superstar Kawhi Leonard.
On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Kim, 55, and Wachtell, Lipton to "conduct a thorough and independent investigation" of allegations that its then-CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort involving his affair with a woman, Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence suspects her of being a spy for China.
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday morning on the heels of a New York Times report that he had also had an extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reports to him.
That allegation could be added to the list of issues that Kim will be looking into as part of his probe.
Nvidia did not immediately respond when asked if the parameters of the investigation would be affected by the new claim. A spokeswoman for Wachtell, Lipton declined to comment for this article on behalf of the firm and Kim.
Friends and former colleagues of Kim said Nvidia has made a smart decision in retaining him for the job.
"I think he's the ideal person for this role," said Edward Kim, a New York white-collar defense lawyer who worked in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York with Joon Kim. The two men are not related.
"I think they're going to get a serious, credible investigation. I believe Joon will follow the facts wherever they will lead," Edward Kim said.
Joon Kim's background
The son of a South Korean diplomat, Joon Kim was born in Los Angeles. He attended Phillips Exeter Academy and later Stanford University.
After graduating cum laude from Harvard Law School, he clerked for a federal judge in Manhattan and then worked as an associate at the major law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton starting in the late 1990s. After that, he spent seven years in the SDNY as an assistant U.S. attorney. His tenure as a prosecutor there included four years in the Organized Crime and Terrorism Unit.
The SDNY, by virtue of its location in Manhattan, handles some of the most high-profile criminal investigations in the United States, including cases of major financial crimes, government corruption and organized crime.
During his first stint at the SDNY, Kim investigated and prosecuted crimes that included "racketeering, murder, money laundering, securities fraud, firearms and narcotics offenses, tax evasion, and terrorism," the office has previously said.
Kim's trial wins at the SDNY included obtaining a conviction of Peter Gotti, then-head of the Gambino Mafia family, for conspiring to kill notorious mob turncoat Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano. Kim and his fellow prosecutors were less successful, however, in prosecuting Peter Gotti's nephew, John Gotti Jr., whose trials ended with several hung juries.
"He could be a very tenacious courtroom advocate," said Chris Conniff, a New York attorney who worked with Kim in the SDNY, and who considers Kim one of his closest friends.
"He's incredibly smart," Conniff said. "I think he's known by everyone in the business as just an outstanding investigator, leaves no stone unturned."
Kim in 2006 returned to Cleary Gottlieb as a partner in the firm's litigation and enforcement group but then went back to the SDNY in 2013. During his second stint there, he served as deputy U.S. attorney, and then served as U.S. attorney from 2017 to 2018.
Kim's elevation to acting U.S. attorney came as a result of President Donald Trump's firing of then-U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara in March 2017 after Bharara refused the new president's demand that he resign.
"Preet's departure was very unique," and the mood in the SDNY "was shaky" after his ouster, Conniff said.
"Preet was very well-liked and well-respected," said Conniff, who was in private practice at the time that Bharara was fired. "We just lost a very charismatic and effective leader, and in a very dramatic way."
In taking over from Bharara, Kim, "from my external viewpoint, he righted the ship and continued to do the work of the office in the time he was there."
"Joon, I would say, gave people confirmation that it was going to be alright, and it was going to be business as usual," Conniff said.
Kim left the SDNY in April 2018, and began his third stint at Cleary Gottlieb, which he recently left to join Wachtell, Lipton's litigation department.
Cuomo and FDIC
In March 2021, Kim and another attorney, Anne Clark, a partner at Vladeck, Raskin & Clark, were tapped by New York Attorney General Letitia James to investigate then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo over allegations that he had sexually harassed several women.
"These are serious allegations that demand a rigorous and impartial investigation," Kim said in a statement at the time. "We will act judiciously and follow the facts wherever they lead."
Kim and Clark in August 2021 submitted a 165-page report to James, which concluded that Cuomo had sexually harassed at least 11 women and then retaliated against a former employee who had publicly complained about his behavior. As part of the probe, Kim, Clark and their team interviewed 179 witnesses and reviewed tens of thousands of documents.
Cuomo adamantly denied some of the allegations and said that other claims of alleged misconduct had been mischaracterized or misinterpreted.
A week after the report was publicly released, Cuomo announced that he would resign.
Two years after the Cuomo probe, Kim was retained by the FDIC to conduct an independent review of allegations of sexual harassment and interpersonal misconduct at the agency. As part of the probe, Kim and his team conducted 167 interviews of current and past FDIC employees, and hundreds of additional interviews with individuals who contacted a hotline the team set up for employees to report misconduct claims.
An April 2024 report by Kim and his team found "for far too many employees and for far too long, the FDIC has failed to provide a workplace safe from sexual harassment, discrimination, and other interpersonal misconduct."
More than five years after Cuomo left office, the former governor's spokesman has not forgotten, or forgiven, Kim, whom he accused of writing a report on Cuomo with a predetermined outcome.
Kim was a "hired hack," said the spokesman, Rich Azzopardi.
Azzopardi said Kim "hid evidence" that was exonerating of Cuomo, and accepted at face value "outright lies" from a number of witnesses.
The bad blood between Cuomo's camp and Kim predates the sexual harassment probe.
While working in the SDNY, Kim and Bharara oversaw the investigation that led to the corruption trial of Joseph Percoco, who had been a close aide of Cuomo. The trial took place after both prosecutors had left the office.
Azzopardi cited that prosecution in his scathing remarks about Kim.
Percoco was sentenced to six years in prison after his 2018 conviction for honest-services wire fraud. The conviction was overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court in a unanimous ruling in 2023 — after his release from prison — because the judge's instructions to jurors were too vague.
Azzopardi said that Kim and Bharara were motivated to prosecute Percoco for "their own personal glory" and "to generate headlines for themselves."
Bharara, in a two-word email response about Azzopardi's claim, wrote, "Andrew who?," referring to Cuomo.
Azzopardi said he did not believe there was any other reason for Nvidia's board to retain Kim to investigate the Huang situation other than to reach a predetermined outcome by the board.
"I don't know what the aims of the board are," Azzopardi said.
Kim's friend Conniff, when asked if he expected that the Nvidia investigation would be a whitewash that would serve the board's interests, said, "No."
"I don't think Joon would take an engagement in which he could not provide a fulsome report of what he uncovered during this investigation," Conniff said. "Any company board that is looking to do a good, thorough investigation of potential wrongdoing, Joon's perfect ... for it."

articles.title: Why Nvidia stock drop isn't a big deal for many ETF, mutual fund investors
articles.text:
Nvidia stock plunged in early trading on Thursday after Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO. Huang co-founded the chipmaker 33 years ago and built it into a behemoth at the center of the artificial intelligence boom.
Since Nvidia is among the largest publicly traded companies by market capitalization, its stock is, by default, a substantial holding in several popular mutual funds and exchange-traded funds.
Many investors therefore hold the chipmaker's stock in their portfolios — and may worry about their exposure.
But mutual fund and ETF investors' exposure to Nvidia stock is likely relatively low, data shows — and any big swings in its stock price are likely to have a fairly muted impact on investor portfolios, financial advisors said.
"This is just a very contemporary, sensational case of risk," said Philip Chao, a certified financial planner and chief investment officer at Experiential Wealth, based in Cabin John, Maryland. "But that is part and parcel to stock investing."
Nvidia's stock fell more than 10% early Thursday on news of Huang's resignation.
Huang stepped down following his admission to having an affair with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China, and after reports that he had a separate extramarital relationship with a direct report, Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare at Nvidia. Reuters also reported Thursday that Huang had an "intimate relationship" with a second Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter.
The stock has since pared some of those losses, and was down more than 5% as of roughly 2:50 p.m. EST.
However, investors "shouldn't worry" about their exposure, Chao said.
For example, if Nvidia were 5% of an overall fund's holdings and the stock dropped 10%, the fund's value would decline 0.5%, assuming all else was equal, Chao said.
"It's not a big deal," he said. "Most people are just reacting to the sensational aspect of this [news]."
A flash poll of members of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council and Financial Advisor 100 on Thursday showed 18 respondents are planning to hold their Nvidia allocations steady in client portfolios. Three are increasing their stake, and six do not own the chipmaker. None of the respondents are decreasing their ownership. The online poll, conducted from 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. ET on Thursday, was sent to 122 firms and 27 responded.
Nvidia's impact on popular ETFs
Let's look at some of the most popular stock ETFs for some specific examples of why investors likely have limited exposure.
1. Vanguard S&P 500 ETF
Nvidia stock is the largest holding in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO).
The fund, as the name suggests, tracks the performance of the S&P 500 U.S. stock index and had a market capitalization of $1.7 trillion as of Sept. 30, according to the most recent Vanguard data.
On that date, Nvidia stock accounted for about 8.4% of the entire portfolio.
Assuming that weighting carried forward to today, a 5% decline in Nvidia's stock would only cause the fund to lose about 0.42% of its value, all else equal, according to an analysis by Experiential Wealth for CNBC.
A 10% decline would lead the fund to drop by 0.84%, according to the analysis.
2. Invesco QQQ Trust
The Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) is an ETF that tracks the performance of the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index.
The fund held about $473.8 billion as of Nov. 10, according to Invesco data.
Nvidia was its second-largest holding, at 6.8% of the overall portfolio. Apple was No. 1, at about 8.4%.
Based on that weighting, the fund would lose just 0.34% of its value if Nvidia's stock lost 5%, all else equal, according to the Experiential Wealth analysis. A 10% Nvidia loss would equate to a 0.68% loss for the overall fund.
3. Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF
Nvidia stock was the largest holding in the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI).
The fund had $1.8 trillion as of Oct. 31, according to Vanguard.
Nvidia stock accounted for about 7.13% of the fund, as of Sept. 30.
According to that weighting, the overall fund would lose roughly 0.36% of its value if Nvidia's stock lost 5%, all else equal, according to Experiential Wealth's analysis. A 10% Nvidia loss would equate to a roughly 0.71% loss for the overall fund.
"There's a difference between [stock] volatility and substantial losses you cannot recover," Chao said.
The Nvidia stock moves fall in the former camp, not the latter, he said.
Average Nvidia exposure in all mutual funds, ETFs
Across all mutual funds and ETFs, "large growth" funds have the largest average weighting to Nvidia stock, according to Morningstar data. These are funds that tend to hold shares in fast-growing U.S. stocks with large market capitalizations.
Large growth funds had an average 10.34% weighting to Nvidia stock as of Wednesday, according to Morningstar. Funds that focus on the technology sector had a 7.31% average weighting to the stock, the second-largest exposure, it found.
Of course, Nvidia stock doesn't exist in a vacuum, financial experts said.
"A 10% Nvidia drop would usually pull down other semiconductor and AI-linked names, such as AMD ... and Micron," Chao said.
And that means mutual fund and ETF losses could be larger than Nvidia holdings might otherwise suggest, he said.
"This event could easily add further pressure to already stretched AI-related stock valuations," Renée Friedman, global head of research at EXANTE, a brokerage firm, wrote in an e-mail.
However, that's not a foregone conclusion, experts said.
The S&P 500 index and the Nasdaq Composite, for example, were down slightly for the day as of about 2:50 p.m. EST.
— CNBC's Sharon Epperson contributed reporting.

articles.title: Watch these levels to know if Nasdaq-100 is set to break out
articles.text: (See the video above for Todd's complete chart breakdown.) Let's get this out of the way. Yes, I'm wearing the stereotypical finance bro vest. Yes, my wife told me it's cringe, and yes, I'm aware that the vest is the official uniform of the finance bro who's about to tell you exactly where the market is headed. I'm not that guy. This finance bro is confident about one thing, and that's that we're in a very uncertain market. Geopolitics, domestic political shift following the midterms, a CEO scandal with the market's most important stock, AI doubts, sticky inflation. Pick your headline. The approach here, I think, is not predicting how it all shakes out. It's being content not knowing, having the confidence to say so, while staying diligent about watching the relationships and levels that matter. Strip out the noise, and the Nasdaq-100 has been doing something pretty boring, actually: chopping in a range since May, roughly 27,200 to 31,000. October's push above the top failed. Last week's flush dipped under the floor and got bought right back up. As long as 27,200 holds, the range is intact. Lose it on a closing basis, and we're having a different conversation. So why can't tech break out? Look under the hood of the 10-year Treasury yield sitting around 5%. Inflation expectations (the orange line) are falling. The bond market is basically saying that the Fed wins the long-term inflation fight. What's doing the heavy lifting is real yields at 2.79% and near their highest since 2008. Real yields are the discount rate for growth stocks, and when they're this high, paying up for future earnings gets a lot harder. That's the headwind, especially for the growth stocks (i.e., semis) that we'll cover next. Now here's where it gets interesting. Look at everything the semis have been dealing with including geopolitical concerns, inflationary pressures outside of energy following that CPI report, domestic political shifts, scandals and Nvidia — which reports earnings next week. Through all that, semiconductors just finished a 32% pullback relative to the S & P 500 . That's almost a carbon copy of the 29% relative drop from mid-2024 into spring of 2025. Last time, that drop marked the low right before a massive run. Does history repeat? I honestly don't know. Remember, I'm not the finance bro in the vest trying to convince you he knows everything. But the setup looks decent. A move back above 0.72 on the SMH/SPY ratio would tell me the leadership is returning to the semis. Until then, keep your head in the game, your eyes wide open, and I'll continue to listen to my wife for dress recommendations on CNBC. Kidding aside, watch the full video for the full explanation of the dynamics at work driving the charts and levels that will spring us into action.
